tbkit.lattice module#

tbkit.lattice.COOR_DTYPE_3D = [('x', 'f8'), ('y', 'f8'), ('z', 'f8'), ('tag', 'U1')]#

Site dtype of a lattice in 3D space (unit_cell and prim_vec given as 3-tuples).

class tbkit.lattice.Lattice(unit_cell: list[dict], prim_vec: list[tuple[float, float]])[source]#

Bases: object

Build up 1D, 2D or 3D lattice. Lattice is defined by the discrete operation:

\[\mathbf{R} = n_1\mathbf{a}_1 + n_2\mathbf{a}_2 + n_3\mathbf{a}_3\]

where \(\mathbf{a}_1\), \(\mathbf{a}_2\), \(\mathbf{a}_3\) are the primitive vectors and \(n_1\), \(n_2\), \(n_3\) are the number of unit cells along them.

Parameters:

  • unit_cell –

    List of dictionaries. One dictionary per site within the unit cell. Each dictionary has two keys:

    • ’tag’, one-character string. Label of the associated sublattice.

    • ’r0’, Tuple. Position: \((x, y)\), or \((x, y, z)\) for a lattice in 3D space.

  • prim_vec – List of tuples. Define the primitive vectors. List of one/two/three tuples for 1D/2D/3D lattices, each the cartesian coordinates of a primitive vector: 2-tuples in the plane, or 3-tuples in 3D space (then r0 must be 3-tuples too, and coor gains a ‘z’ field, see COOR_DTYPE_3D).

In 3D space, the geometry methods acting in the plane (rotation, ellipse_in, boundary_line, …) act on \((x, y)\) only (rotation about the z axis, cylinders, vertical planes), and plot draws the projection on the \((x, y)\) plane.

Example usage:

# Line-Centered Square lattice
unit_cell = [{'tag': 'a', 'r0': (0., 0.)}, {'tag': 'a', 'r0': (0., 1.)}]
prim_vec = [(0, 2), (2, 0)]
lat = lattice(unit_cell=unit_cell, prim_vec=prim_vec)
get_lattice(n1: int, n2: int = 1, n3: int = 1) → None[source]#

Get the lattice positions, sorted by (y, x) – by (z, y, x) in 3D space.

Parameters:

  • n1 – Positive Integer. Number of unit cells along \(\mathbf{a}_1\).

  • n2 – Positive Integer. Default value 1. Number of unit cells along \(\mathbf{a}_2\).

  • n3 – Positive Integer. Default value 1. Number of unit cells along \(\mathbf{a}_3\) (3D lattices only).

Example usage:

# Line-Centered Square lattice
unit_cell = [{'tag': 'a', 'r0': (0., 0.)}, {'tag': 'a', 'r0': (0., 1.)}]
prim_vec = [(0, 2), (2, 0)]
lat = lattice(unit_cell=unit_cell, prim_vec=prim_vec)
lat.get_lattice(n1=4, n2=5)

tbkit.system module#

class tbkit.system.System(lat: Lattice)[source]#

Bases: object

Solve the Tight-Binding eigenvalue problem of a lattice defined by the class lattice.

Parameters:

lat – lattice class instance.

Up to dense_max sites (default 5000), the distances between all pairs of sites are computed (and kept in vec_hop). Larger lattices only look for the neighbours they need, with a k-d tree, up to the largest neighbour order a call asks for: memory and time then grow linearly with the number of sites (vec_hop stays empty).

dense_max = 5000#

Largest lattice (number of sites) whose pairwise distances are all computed.

clear_hopping() → None[source]#

Clear structured array hop.

get_distances(n_orders: int = 1) → None[source]#

Private method. Get distances and angles of the edges. The angle is that of the bond’s projection on the (x, y) plane; in 3D space, a vertical bond gets angle 0 pointing up (+z) and -180 pointing down.

Parameters:

n_orders – Positive integer. Default value 1. Beyond dense_max sites, the number of neighbour orders (distinct distances) needed.

print_distances(n: int = 1) → None[source]#

Print distances and positive angles (in degrees) \(\phi_+\in[0, 180)\) of the nth shortest edges. Negative angles are given by: \(\phi_-= \phi_+-180\) and \(\phi_-\in[-180, 0)\).

Parameters:

n – Positive integer. Number of shortest edges.

set_onsite(dict_onsite: dict[str, complex]) → None[source]#

Set onsite energies.

Parameters:

dict_onsite – Dictionary. key: sublattice tag, val: onsite energy.

Example usage:

# Line-Centered Square lattice
sys.set_onsite({'a': -1j, 'b': -2j})
get_bonds(n: int) → tuple[NDArray, NDArray, NDArray][source]#

Private method. Get every bond of the nth shortest length once, oriented from i to j so that its angle lies in \([0, 180)\).

The sign of hop[‘ang’] is what marks a hopping as belonging to the upper or the lower part of the Hamiltonian (see get_ham). Sites sorted by (y, x), as get_lattice leaves them, give that orientation for \(i < j\), but rotation, clean_coor, +=, … reorder the sites, so the orientation is taken from the angle itself.

Returns:

  • i, j – Integer ndarrays. Bond end points.

  • ang – Real ndarray. Bond angles, in degrees, in \([0, 180)\).

fill_store_hop(n: int) → None[source]#

Private method.

Store in store_hop indices, positive angles, and tags of a given type of hopping (see get_bonds).

set_hopping(list_hop: list[dict], upper_part: bool = True) → None[source]#

Set lattice hoppings.

Parameters:

  • list_hop –

    List of Dictionaries. Dictionary with keys (‘n’, ‘ang’, ‘tag’, ‘t’) where:

    • ’n’ Positive integer, type of hoppings:

      • ’n’: 1 for nearest neighbours.

      • ’n’: 2 for next-nearest neighbours.

      • ’n’: 3 for next-next-nearest neighbours.

      • etc…

    • ’ang’ value, float, angle, in deg, of the hoppings. (optional).

      Hopping angles are given by the method print_distances.

      • If \(ang \in[0, 180)\), fill the Hamiltonian upper part.

      • If \(ang \in[-180, 0)\), fill the Hamiltonian lower part.

    • ’tag’ string of length 2 (optional).

      Hopping tags.

    • ’t’ Complex number.

      Hopping value.

  • upper_part –

    Boolean. Default value True.

    • True, get the hoppings with angles in \([0, 180)\), i.e. fill the Hamiltonian upper part.

    • False, get the reversed hoppings, with angles in \([-180, 0)\), i.e. fill the Hamiltonian lower part.

Example usage:

# fill upper part:
sys.set_hopping([{'n': 1, 't': 1.}])
# fill lower part:
sys.set_hopping([{'n': 1, 't': 1.}], upper_part=False)
# fill upper part: specifying the angles:
sys.set_hopping([{'n': 1, 'ang': 0., 't': 1.}, {'n': 1, 'ang': 90., 't': 2.}])
# fill lower part:
sys.set_hopping([{'n': 1, 'ang': -180., 't': 1.}, {'n': 1, 'ang': -90., 't': 2.}],
                           upper_part=False)
# fill upper part: specifying the tags:
sys.set_hopping([{'n': 1, 'tag': 'ab', 't': 1.}, {'n': 1, 'tag': 'ba', 't': 2.}])
# fill lower part:
sys.set_hopping([{'n': 1, 'tag': 'ab', 't': 1.}, {'n': 1, 'tag': 'ba', 't': 2.}],
                           upper_part=False)
# fill upper part: specifying the angles and tags:
sys.set_hopping([{'n': 1, 'ang': 0., 'tag': 'ab', 't': 1.},
                            {'n': 1, 'ang': 0., 'tag': 'ba', 't': 2.},
                            {'n': 1, 'ang': 90., 'tag': 'ab', 't': 3.},
                            {'n': 1, 'ang': 90., 'tag': 'ba', 't': 4.}])
# fill lower part:
sys.set_hopping([{'n': 1, 'ang': -180., 'tag': 'ab', 't': 1.},
                            {'n': 1, 'ang': -180., 'tag': 'ba', 't': 2.},
                            {'n': 1, 'ang': -90., 'tag': 'ab', 't': 3.},
                            {'n': 1, 'ang': -90., 'tag': 'ba', 't': 4.}],
                           upper_part=False)

Note

A Hermitian hopping matrix can be built using only its upper part OR only its lower part. The full matrix is then built automatically by Hermitian conjugation.

If both the upper AND the lower parts are used to build the hopping matrix, no Hermitian conjugation is performed, i.e. a non-Hermitian hopping matrix can be built.

set_peierls_phase(phase: Callable[[...], NDArray]) → None[source]#

Apply the Peierls substitution to the existing hoppings, to capture the effect of an orbital magnetic field:

\[t_{ij} \to t_{ij}\, e^{i\phi_{ij}}\, ,\quad \phi_{ij} = \frac{2\pi}{\Phi_0}\int_{\mathbf{r}_i}^{\mathbf{r}_j} \mathbf{A}\cdot d\mathbf{l}\]

where \(\mathbf{A}\) is the vector potential, integrated along the straight bond from site \(i\) to site \(j\).

Must be called after set_hopping / set_hopping_manual (it rescales the existing hoppings in place) and before get_ham. For a uniform perpendicular field, use the convenience method set_magnetic_field instead.

Parameters:

phase – Callable. phase(xi, yi, xj, yj) returns \(\phi_{ij}\), the (real-valued) Peierls phase for the bond from \((x_i, y_i)\) to \((x_j, y_j)\). Called with Numpy arrays (one value per hopping in sys.hop).

Note

get_ham automatically assigns the reversed bond its complex conjugate, so the Hamiltonian stays Hermitian as long as phase is antisymmetric under swapping \(i\) and \(j\) – true for the line integral of any vector potential, since reversing the integration path negates it.

Example usage:

# Peierls phase from a uniform field via the Landau gauge
# A = (0, B x): the same field as set_magnetic_field(alpha),
# just in a different (equally valid) gauge.
alpha = 0.01
sys.set_peierls_phase(lambda xi, yi, xj, yj:
                                  2 * np.pi * alpha * (yj - yi) * (xi + xj) / 2)
set_magnetic_field(alpha: float) → None[source]#

Set a uniform perpendicular magnetic field via the Peierls substitution (see set_peierls_phase), using the symmetric gauge \(\mathbf{A} = \frac{B}{2}(-y, x)\):

\[\phi_{ij} = \pi\alpha\,(x_iy_j - x_jy_i)\]
Parameters:

alpha – Real number. Flux density \(B/\Phi_0\), in flux quanta per unit area (in the lattice’s length units) – i.e. the flux through a region of area \(S\) is \(\alpha S\) flux quanta.

Example usage:

# one flux quantum per 100 unit cells of a lattice with
# lattice constant 1:
sys.set_magnetic_field(alpha=0.01)
set_onsite_dis(alpha: complex) → None[source]#

set_hopping_def(hopping_def: dict[tuple[int, int], complex]) → None[source]#

Set specific hoppings.

Parameters:

hopping_def – Dictionary of hoppings. key: hopping indices \((i, j)\), val: hopping value \(t_{ij}\). If sys.hop stores the bond the other way round, as \((j, i)\) (only one direction is stored for a Hermitian Hamiltonian), that entry is set to \(t_{ij}^*\), so that \(H_{ij} = t_{ij}\). A pair that is not a hopping of sys.hop is ignored.

Example usage:

get_eig(eigenvec: bool = False, left: bool = False) → None[source]#

Get the eigenergies, eigenvectors and polarisation.

Parameters:

  • eigenvec – Boolean. Default value False. If True, get the eigenvectors.

  • left – Boolean. Default value False. If True, get the left eigenvectors too. Relevant for non-Hermitian matrices.

get_eig_sparse(n_eig: int = 10, sigma: complex = 0.0, eigenvec: bool = False) → None[source]#

Get the n_eig eigenenergies closest to sigma, and optionally their eigenvectors, with the sparse shift-invert Lanczos (Hermitian) or Arnoldi (non-Hermitian) solver of ARPACK. Unlike get_eig, it never builds the dense matrix, so it reaches lattices of \(10^5\) sites and more – e.g. the states near a band centre, or the zero modes of a large flake. The results replace en (sorted by real part) and, with eigenvec, rn, intensity and pola, as for get_eig.

Parameters:

  • n_eig – Positive integer. Default value 10. Number of eigenpairs (at most sites - 2).

  • sigma – Real or complex number. Default value 0. Target energy (if it is exactly an eigenvalue, it is shifted by about 1e-9).

  • eigenvec – Boolean. Default value False.

get_green(energy: complex, eta: float = 1e-06) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

Get the retarded Green’s function (resolvent)

\[G(E) = \left[(E + i\eta) - H\right]^{-1}\, .\]
Parameters:

  • energy – Real (or complex) number. Energy \(E\).

  • eta – Positive real or zero. Default value 1e-6. Broadening \(\eta\).

Returns:

  • G – Complex ndarray, shape (sites, sites).

get_ldos(energies: ArrayLike, eta: float = 0.05) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the local density of states

\[\rho_i(E) = -\frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{Im}\,G_{ii}(E) = \sum_n |\psi_n(i)|^2\,\frac{\eta/\pi}{(E - E_n)^2 + \eta^2}\]

(the second form, from the eigenvectors, for a Hermitian Hamiltonian). Summed over sites it is the Lorentzian-broadened density of states.

Parameters:

  • energies – Real array. Energies.

  • eta – Positive real. Default value 0.05. Broadening.

Returns:

  • ldos – Real ndarray, shape (len(energies), sites).

get_fermi_level(n_electrons: float, temperature: float = 0.0) → float[source]#

Get the Fermi level holding n_electrons electrons in the spectrum en (one electron per state; see tbkit.occupation.fermi_level).

Parameters:

  • temperature – Positive real or zero. Default value 0.

Returns:

  • e_fermi – Real number.

get_charge_density(e_fermi: float, temperature: float = 0.0) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the electron density on every site, \(n_i = \sum_n f(E_n)\,|\psi_n(i)|^2\).

Parameters:

  • temperature – Positive real or zero. Default value 0.

Returns:

  • density – Real ndarray, shape (sites,).

get_total_energy(e_fermi: float, temperature: float = 0.0) → float[source]#

Get the band energy \(E = \sum_n f(E_n)\,E_n\).

Parameters:

  • e_fermi – Real number. Fermi level.

  • temperature – Positive real or zero. Default value 0.

Returns:

  • energy – Real number.

get_ipr() → None[source]#

Get the Inverse Participation Ratio:

\[IPR_n = \sum_i|\psi_i^{n}|^4\, .\]
get_petermann() → None[source]#

Get the Petermann factor:

\[K_n = \frac{\langle\psi_L^{n}|\psi_L^{n}\rangle\langle\psi_R^{n}|\psi_R^{n}\rangle}{|\langle\psi_L^{n}|\psi_R^{n}\rangle|^2}\, .\]

Note

LA.eig fixes the norm such that \(\langle\psi_L^{n}|\psi_L^{n}\rangle = 1\) and \(\langle\psi_R^{n}|\psi_R^{n}\rangle = 1\).

get_intensity_pola_max(tag_pola: str) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the state with largest polarization on one sublattice.

get_intensity_pola_min(tag_pola: str) → NDArray[float64][source]#

tag_pola – One-character string. Sublattice tag.

Returns:

get_intensity_en(lims: tuple[float, float]) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get, if any, the intensity of the sum of the states whose energies (real part) lie between lims[0] and lims[1].

Parameters:

lims – List. lims[0] energy min, lims[1] energy max.

Returns:

  • intensity – Sum of the intensities between (lims[0], lims[1]).

get_local_chern_marker(e_fermi: float = 0.0, area: float | None = None) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the local Chern marker of the states below e_fermi (Bianco and Resta, Phys. Rev. B 84, 241106 (2011)),

\[C(\mathbf{r}_i) = -\frac{4\pi}{a}\,\mathrm{Im}\, \langle i|\,P\,x\,Q\,y\,P\,|i\rangle\, ,\]

with \(P\) the projector on the occupied states, \(Q = 1-P\), and \(a\) the area per site. Averaged over the bulk of a finite flake – even a disordered or amorphous one, where no Brillouin zone exists – it gives the Chern number, in the sign convention of KSpace.chern_number; it sums to zero over the whole flake, the edges carrying the opposite value.

Parameters:

  • e_fermi – Real number. Default value 0. Fermi energy: the states with energies below it are occupied.

  • area – Positive real number. Default value None: the area of the unit cell of lat divided by its number of sites.

Returns:

  • marker – Real ndarray, shape (sites,).

Pauli matrices (plus the identity, key '0'), for building spinful hoppings/onsite terms (spin-orbit coupling, Zeeman splitting, …) when KSpace is constructed with spin=True.

tbkit.kspace.reciprocal_vectors(prim_vec: list[tuple[float, ...]]) → list[tuple[float, ...]][source]#

Get the reciprocal lattice vectors \(\mathbf{b}_i\) such that \(\mathbf{a}_i\cdot\mathbf{b}_j = 2\pi\delta_{ij}\), lying in the span of the \(\mathbf{a}_i\).

Parameters:

prim_vec – List of one/two/three tuples. Primitive vectors (see class lattice).

Returns:

  • rec_vec – List of one/two/three tuples. Reciprocal vectors, with as many components as the primitive vectors.

class tbkit.kspace.KSpace(lat: Lattice, spin: bool = False)[source]#

Bases: object

Build and solve the Tight-Binding Bloch Hamiltonian \(H(\mathbf{k})\) of a periodic lattice defined by the class lattice.

Hoppings are defined between orbitals of the unit cell, separated by a lattice vector \(\mathbf{R} = n_1\mathbf{a}_1+n_2\mathbf{a}_2\):

\[H_{ij}(\mathbf{k}) = \sum_{\mathbf{R}} t_{ij}(\mathbf{R})\, e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}}\]
Parameters:

  • lat – lattice class instance. Only unit_cell and prim_vec are used (the instance need not call get_lattice).

  • spin – Boolean. Default value False. If True, every site of unit_cell carries a spin-1/2 degree of freedom (norb doubles to 2*len(unit_cell), ordered site-major: orbitals 2*i, 2*i+1 are the up/down components of site i). set_onsite and set_hopping then accept 2x2 (spin) matrices in addition to plain numbers, to build spin-orbit coupling or Zeeman terms – see PAULI for ready-made Pauli matrices.

Example usage:

# graphene, nearest-neighbor hopping t
DX, DY = 0.5 * 3 ** 0.5, 0.5
unit_cell = [{'tag': 'a', 'r0': (0., 0.)}, {'tag': 'b', 'r0': (DX, DY)}]
prim_vec = [(2*DX, 0.), (DX, 1.5)]
lat = Lattice(unit_cell=unit_cell, prim_vec=prim_vec)
gra = KSpace(lat)
gra.set_hopping([{'i': 0, 'j': 1, 'R': (0, 0), 't': 1.},
                        {'i': 0, 'j': 1, 'R': (-1, 0), 't': 1.},
                        {'i': 0, 'j': 1, 'R': (0, -1), 't': 1.}])
rec_vec_k#

Reciprocal vectors in the k coordinates used by get_ham (rows).

set_onsite(dict_onsite: dict[str, complex | Sequence[complex]]) → None[source]#

Set the onsite energies, by sublattice tag.

Parameters:

dict_onsite – Dictionary. key: tag, val: onsite energy (a plain number), or, if spin=True, a plain number (applied equally to both spins), a pair (E_up, E_down) of numbers (a spin splitting along z), or a 2x2 complex matrix (a general spin structure, e.g. an in-plane Zeeman field built from PAULI). A complex onsite energy (gain/loss), or a non-Hermitian 2x2 block, makes \(H(\mathbf{k})\) non-Hermitian: get_bands then returns complex energies, sorted by their real part.

Example usage:

kag.set_onsite({'a': 1., 'b': -1.})
# spinful: same onsite energy for both spins on 'a', a Zeeman
# splitting along z on 'b':
kag_spin.set_onsite({'a': 1., 'b': (1., -1.)})
# spinful: an in-plane Zeeman field on 'a':
kag_spin.set_onsite({'a': Bx*PAULI['x']})
set_hopping(list_hop: list[dict], hermitian: bool = True) → None[source]#

Set the hoppings between orbitals of the unit cell.

Only one representative of each hopping needs to be given: its Hermitian conjugate (\(j\to i\), \(\mathbf{R}\to-\mathbf{R}\)) is added automatically (unless hermitian=False).

Parameters:

  • list_hop –

    List of dictionaries with keys (‘i’, ‘j’, ‘R’, ‘t’):

    • ’i’, ‘j’: Positive integers. Site indices within the unit cell (following the order of unit_cell).

    • ’R’: Tuple of one/two integers \((n_1, n_2)\). Lattice vector \(\mathbf{R}=n_1\mathbf{a}_1+n_2\mathbf{a}_2\) separating the two sites.

    • ’t’: Complex number, or, if spin=True, either a complex number (spin-independent hopping) or a 2x2 complex matrix (a general, possibly spin-mixing, hopping – e.g. built from PAULI for Rashba or intrinsic spin-orbit coupling).

  • hermitian – Boolean. Default value True. If False, the Hermitian conjugates are not added: each dictionary is one matrix element \(H_{ij}(\mathbf{R})\) only, so that non-reciprocal (non-Hermitian) hoppings can be built – give the reverse hopping explicitly, with its own amplitude.

Example usage:

# 1D chain, nearest-neighbor hopping t between the only orbital
# and its right neighbor:
chain.set_hopping([{'i': 0, 'j': 0, 'R': (1,), 't': 1.}])
# spinful: spin-independent hopping t, plus a Rashba-like
# spin-flip term of strength alpha:
chain_spin.set_hopping([{'i': 0, 'j': 0, 'R': (1,),
                                        't': t*PAULI['0'] + 1j*alpha*PAULI['y']}])
set_overlap(list_hop: list[dict]) → None[source]#

Set the overlaps \(s_{ij}(\mathbf{R}) = \langle i,\mathbf{0}|j,\mathbf{R}\rangle\) of a non-orthogonal basis, in the format of set_hopping (key ‘t’ for the overlap; the Hermitian conjugates are added):

\[S(\mathbf{k}) = \mathbb{1} + \sum_{\mathbf{R}} s(\mathbf{R})\,e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}}\, ,\]

after which the bands solve \(H(\mathbf{k})v = E\,S(\mathbf{k})v\). (With graphene’s nearest-neighbour overlap \(s\), the \(\pi\) bands become \(E = (\epsilon \pm t|f|)/(1 \pm s|f|)\): no longer symmetric about \(\epsilon\).) The topological tools use the Lowdin-orthonormalized states \(S^{1/2}v\).

Parameters:

list_hop – List of dictionaries (‘i’, ‘j’, ‘R’, ‘t’), see set_hopping.

get_overlap(k: ArrayLike) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

Parameters:

k – k point (see get_ham).

Returns:

  • S – Complex ndarray, shape (norb, norb).

clear_hopping() → None[source]#

Clear the hoppings set by set_hopping (and the overlaps of set_overlap).

get_ham(k: ArrayLike) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

Get the dense Bloch Hamiltonian \(H(\mathbf{k})\).

Parameters:

k – Tuple/list/ndarray of dim real numbers. When the lattice fills its space (2D in the plane, 3D in space), the \(\mathbf{k}\) point in the same Cartesian frame as prim_vec. In 1D, the crystal momentum along the primitive vector (so the Brillouin zone spans \(2\pi/|\mathbf{a}_1|\)), which coincides with \(k_x\) for a chain aligned with \(x\). For a 2D lattice in 3D space (a slab), the components along the orthonormal basis k_basis of its plane (the first along \(\mathbf{a}_1\)). rec_vec_k holds the reciprocal vectors in these coordinates.

Returns:

  • ham – Complex ndarray, shape (norb, norb).

get_ham_peierls(k: ArrayLike, A: ArrayLike) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

Get the Bloch Hamiltonian in a uniform vector potential \(\mathbf{A}\) (\(\hbar = e = 1\)): every hopping picks up the Peierls phase \(e^{i\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{d}}\) of its bond vector \(\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{R} + \boldsymbol\tau_j - \boldsymbol\tau_i\) (see System.set_peierls_phase). A time-dependent \(\mathbf{A}(t)\) is a uniform electric field \(-\partial_t\mathbf{A}\), e.g. light (see tbkit.floquet).

Parameters:

  • k – k point (see get_ham).

  • A – Tuple/ndarray of space_dim real numbers. Vector potential.

Returns:

  • ham – Complex ndarray, shape (norb, norb).

get_bands(ks: ArrayLike, eigenvec: bool = False) → NDArray[float64] | tuple[NDArray[float64], NDArray[complex128]][source]#

Diagonalize \(H(\mathbf{k})\) over a set of k-points, and keep the result for plot_bands (plotted against the cumulative distance between consecutive k-points).

Parameters:

  • ks – ndarray, shape (nk, dim). k-points.

  • eigenvec – Boolean. Default value False. If True, also return the eigenvectors.

Returns:

  • en – Real ndarray, shape (nk, norb). Band energies, sorted ascending. Complex, and sorted by real part, if \(H(\mathbf{k})\) is non-Hermitian (complex onsite energies, see set_onsite).

  • vn – Complex ndarray, shape (nk, norb, norb), only if eigenvec is True. vn[k, :, n] is the nth (right) eigenvector at ks[k].

Check whether \(H(\mathbf{k})\) is Hermitian: it is, unless an onsite term is not, or set_hopping was called with hermitian=False (such a model is always treated as non-Hermitian, and diagonalized with the general solver).

berry_curvature(bands: int | list[int], nk: int | tuple[int, int] = 30, plane: tuple[int, int] = (0, 1), k_fixed: float = 0.0) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the Berry curvature of a group of bands over a uniform Brillouin-zone mesh, using the gauge-invariant lattice method of Fukui, Hatsugai and Suzuki (J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 74, 1674 (2005)): the flux through each mesh plaquette is minus the phase of the product of the (Slater-determinant) overlaps between the occupied subspaces at its four corners,

\[\Omega_{\square} = -\arg\prod_{\langle\mathbf{k}\mathbf{k}'\rangle\in\partial\square} \det\langle u(\mathbf{k})|u(\mathbf{k}')\rangle\, ,\]

the corners being visited counterclockwise. This is the discrete version of \(\Omega = \partial_{k_x}A_y - \partial_{k_y}A_x\), \(\mathbf{A} = i\langle u|\nabla_{\mathbf{k}}u\rangle\), and does not depend on the orientation (handedness) of prim_vec. The local curvature is that of the periodic gauge of get_ham (orbitals on the cell origin), which differs point by point from the one with the orbital positions included (see quantum_geometric_tensor); their integral, the Chern number, is the same. For a non-Hermitian \(H(\mathbf{k})\) (see set_onsite), the bands are ordered by the real part of their energy and the overlaps are taken between right eigenvectors (the “RR” curvature of biorthogonal_berry_curvature). That ordering follows the bands continuously only if a real line gap separates bands from the others over the whole zone: without one (an imaginary line gap, or exceptional points), a ValueError is raised instead of a meaningless result – see biorthogonal_berry_curvature.

Parameters:

  • bands – Positive integer, or list of positive integers. Band index, or indices of a group of bands (e.g. all occupied bands below a gap).

  • nk – Positive integer, or tuple of 2 positive integers. Default value 30. Number of k-points along each of the two reciprocal lattice vectors spanning the plane.

  • plane – Tuple of two distinct integers. Default value (0, 1). 3D lattices only: the reciprocal vectors \(\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{b}_j\) spanning the plane of the Brillouin zone. The flux is oriented along the remaining primitive vector \(\mathbf{a}_l\) (along +z in 2D).

  • k_fixed – Real number. Default value 0. 3D lattices only: the fractional coordinate of the plane along the remaining reciprocal vector \(\mathbf{b}_l\) (e.g. \(k_z\) in units of \(|\mathbf{b}_3|\) for plane=(0, 1)).

Returns:

  • curv – Real ndarray, shape (nk1, nk2). Berry curvature (flux through each plaquette, in radians). Summing curv and dividing by \(2\pi\) gives the Chern number, see chern_number.

biorthogonal_berry_curvature(bands: int | list[int], nk: int | tuple[int, int] = 30, kind: str = 'LR', gap: str = 'real', plane: tuple[int, int] = (0, 1), k_fixed: float = 0.0) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the Berry curvature of a group of bands of a (non-Hermitian) model from its right and left eigenvectors, \(H|R_n\rangle = E_n|R_n\rangle\) and \(H^\dagger|L_n\rangle = E_n^*|L_n\rangle\), normalized by \(\langle L_m|R_n\rangle = \delta_{mn}\) (Shen, Zhen and Fu, Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 146402 (2018)). The four connections

\[\mathbf{A}^{\alpha\beta} = i\langle u^\alpha|\nabla_{\mathbf{k}}u^\beta\rangle\, , \qquad \alpha, \beta \in \{L, R\}\, ,\]

have different curvatures point by point, but their integrals, the Chern numbers \(C^{LR} = C^{RL} = C^{RR} = C^{LL}\), are the same integer. The flux through each plaquette is computed as in berry_curvature (Fukui-Hatsugai-Suzuki), with the links \(\det\langle u^\alpha(\mathbf{k})|u^\beta(\mathbf{k}')\rangle\) (for RR and LL, the phase does not depend on the normalization). For a Hermitian model all four are the curvature of berry_curvature.

The bands are ordered at every k-point by the real part of their energy (gap = ‘real’) or by its imaginary part (‘imaginary’), and bands must be separated from the others by a line gap of that kind over the whole zone – a line \(\mathrm{Re}\,E = E_0\) (or \(\mathrm{Im}\,E = E_0\)) that no band crosses. Otherwise a ValueError is raised: the gap closes at exceptional points (see tbkit.exceptional.find_exceptional_points), where the Chern number can change.

Parameters:

  • bands – Positive integer, or list of positive integers. Band indices in the order set by gap.

  • nk – Positive integer, or tuple of 2 positive integers. Default value 30. See berry_curvature.

  • kind – ‘LR’, ‘RL’, ‘RR’ or ‘LL’. Default value ‘LR’. \(\alpha\beta\) above.

  • gap – ‘real’ or ‘imaginary’. Default value ‘real’. Kind of line gap, and the order of the bands.

  • plane – Tuple of two integers. Default value (0, 1). 3D only, see berry_curvature.

  • k_fixed – Real number. Default value 0. 3D only, see berry_curvature.

Returns:

  • curv – Real ndarray, shape (nk1, nk2). Flux through each plaquette, in radians (sign convention of berry_curvature).

biorthogonal_chern_number(bands: int | list[int], nk: int | tuple[int, int] = 30, kind: str = 'LR', gap: str = 'real', plane: tuple[int, int] = (0, 1), k_fixed: float = 0.0) → float[source]#

Get the Chern number of a line-gapped group of bands of a (non-Hermitian) model, \(C^{\alpha\beta} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{BZ} \Omega^{\alpha\beta}\,d^2k\), the same integer for the four kinds LR, RL, RR, LL (see biorthogonal_berry_curvature). It equals the Hermitian Chern number of chern_number as long as the line gap stays open.

Parameters:

  • bands – See biorthogonal_berry_curvature.

  • nk – See biorthogonal_berry_curvature.

  • kind – ‘LR’, ‘RL’, ‘RR’ or ‘LL’. Default value ‘LR’.

  • gap – ‘real’ or ‘imaginary’. Default value ‘real’.

  • plane – See berry_curvature.

  • k_fixed – See berry_curvature.

Returns:

  • chern – Real number, close to an integer.

chern_number(bands: int | list[int], nk: int | tuple[int, int] = 30, plane: tuple[int, int] = (0, 1), k_fixed: float = 0.0) → float[source]#

Get the Chern number of a group of bands:

\[C = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{BZ} \Omega(\mathbf{k})\, d^2k\]

an integer (up to the numerical precision set by nk) for a group of bands that is isolated from the rest of the spectrum by a gap everywhere in the Brillouin zone. See berry_curvature. For a non-Hermitian model, bands (ordered by Re E) must be isolated by a real line gap, or a ValueError is raised; biorthogonal_chern_number also handles imaginary line gaps and the left eigenvectors.

Parameters:

  • bands – Positive integer, or list of positive integers. Band index, or indices of a group of bands (e.g. all occupied bands below a gap).

  • nk – Positive integer, or tuple of 2 positive integers. Default value 30. Number of k-points along each reciprocal lattice vector.

  • plane – Tuple of two integers. Default value (0, 1). 3D lattices only, see berry_curvature.

  • k_fixed – Real number. Default value 0. 3D lattices only, see berry_curvature: the Chern number of the plane at this fractional coordinate (it jumps across a Weyl point).

Returns:

  • chern – Real number, close to an integer.

hall_conductivity(e_fermi: float | ArrayLike, temperature: float = 0.0, nk: int | tuple[int, ...] = 60, plane: tuple[int, int] = (0, 1), k_fixed: float | None = None, positions: bool = True, refine: int = 1, refine_fraction: float = 0.05) → float | NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity at any Fermi level – in a gap, in a band, or at a band crossing – from the Kubo formula over a uniform Brillouin-zone mesh,

\[\sigma_{xy} = \frac{e^2}{\hbar}\int_{BZ}\frac{d^dk}{(2\pi)^d}\, F(\mathbf{k})\, ,\qquad F = -\sum_{n\neq m}(f_n - f_m)\, \frac{\mathrm{Im}\left[\langle n|\partial_x H|m\rangle\langle m|\partial_y H|n\rangle\right]} {(E_n - E_m)^2} = \sum_n f_n\,\Omega_n\, ,\]

with \(f_n = f(E_n)\) the Fermi-Dirac occupations and

\[\Omega_n = -2\,\mathrm{Im}\sum_{m\neq n} \frac{\langle n|\partial_x H|m\rangle\langle m|\partial_y H|n\rangle}{(E_n-E_m)^2} = -2\,\mathrm{Im}\langle\partial_x u_n|\partial_y u_n\rangle\]

the Berry curvature of band n (\(\partial_\mu H = \partial H/\partial k_\mu\), the convention \(\Omega = \partial_xA_y - \partial_yA_x\), \(\mathbf{A} = i\langle u|\nabla_{\mathbf{k}}u\rangle\) of berry_curvature). The form with \(f_n - f_m\) stays finite where bands touch: degenerate pairs have equal occupations and drop out, instead of cancelling between two diverging \(\Omega_n\). \(\partial H/\partial\mathbf{k}\) is built analytically from the stored hoppings, \(\sum_{\mathbf{R}} i\mathbf{d}\,t\,e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{d}}\) with the Cartesian bond vector \(\mathbf{d}\).

Sign. In a gap, \(\sigma_{xy} = C\,e^2/h\) with \(C\) the value chern_number returns for the occupied bands: this is the sign of TKNN (Phys. Rev. Lett. 49, 405 (1982)), whose \(\sigma_H = (e^2/h)\,\frac{i}{2\pi}\int d^2k\,(\langle\partial_1u|\partial_2u\rangle - \langle\partial_2u|\partial_1u\rangle)\) has the same integrand, \(\Omega/2\pi\). The adiabatic (semiclassical) response of a charge \(q\) of either sign, \(\dot{\mathbf{r}} = \partial_{\mathbf{k}}E - \dot{\mathbf{k}}\times\boldsymbol\Omega\) with \(\hbar\dot{\mathbf{k}} = q\mathbf{E}\), gives the opposite sign for the tensor of Ohm’s law \(j_x = \sigma^{\mathrm{Ohm}}_{xy}E_y\): \(\sigma^{\mathrm{Ohm}}_{xy} = -(q^2/\hbar)\int F\,d^dk/(2\pi)^d\), the convention of Wang, Yates, Souza and Vanderbilt (Phys. Rev. B 74, 195118 (2006)) and of the Kubo-Bastin formula (tbkit.kpm.hall_conductivity returns, likewise, minus it). So the value returned is \(\sigma^{\mathrm{Ohm}}_{yx} = -\sigma^{\mathrm{Ohm}}_{xy}\); e.g. a massive Dirac cone \(v(k_x\sigma_x + k_y\sigma_y) + m\sigma_z\) gives \(+\frac{e^2}{2h}\frac{m}{|E_F|}\) outside its gap (the literature’s \(\sigma_{xy} = -\frac{e^2}{2h}\frac{m}{|E_F|}\)), and \(\frac{e^2}{2h}\mathrm{sgn}(m)\) inside.

Orbital positions. The velocity is \(\partial H/\partial\mathbf{k}\) in the gauge of positions: with positions=True (the default) the bond vector is \(\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{R} + \boldsymbol\tau_j - \boldsymbol\tau_i\), the matrix of the physical velocity \(i[H, \mathbf{r}]\) of a tight-binding model whose position operator is diagonal on its orbitals (the one kpm.hall_conductivity uses on a torus). With positions=False, every orbital sits on its cell origin (the periodic gauge of get_ham). The two differ by \(i(E_n-E_m)\langle n|\boldsymbol\tau|m\rangle\) in the velocity’s matrix elements, so the band curvatures differ by \(\nabla\times\langle n|\boldsymbol\tau|n\rangle\), a total derivative: the conductivities agree whenever the bands below \(E_F\) are all full (in a gap, at any temperature well below the gap) and differ in general at partial filling, by the circulation \(\frac{1}{2\pi}\oint_{FS}\langle n|\boldsymbol\tau|n\rangle\cdot d\mathbf{k}\) around the Fermi surface. The default is the physical one.

Units and dimensions. In 2D, \(\sigma\) is in units of \(e^2/h\) (\(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int d^2k\,F\)). In 3D, with k_fixed given, the value of the plane (the conductance of that slice of the Brillouin zone, in \(e^2/h\), oriented like chern_number along \(\mathbf{a}_l\)); with k_fixed=None, the full 3D conductivity as the Hall (pseudo)vector \((\sigma_{yz}, \sigma_{zx}, \sigma_{xy}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^2}\int d^3k\,\mathbf{F}\) in units of \(e^2/(h\cdot\mathrm{length})\) (length the unit of prim_vec): \(\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_l\bar C_l\,\mathbf{b}_l\), e.g. \(C/c\) along \(z\) for a stack of Chern layers \(c\) apart.

Convergence. The integrand peaks where bands nearly touch close to \(E_F\) (hot spots), and jumps across the Fermi surface. A temperature smooths the latter. refine resamples the fraction refine_fraction of mesh cells with the largest \(|F|\) on a finer submesh (refine points per direction), in the spirit of the adaptive mesh refinement of Wang, Yates, Souza and Vanderbilt (2006); the cells are ranked by the size of the curvature whatever the occupations. It is meant for metals: in a gap the plain uniform mesh already converges exponentially, and refining part of it costs a little accuracy (about \(4\cdot10^{-4}\) for the Haldane model on a 60 x 60 mesh). With an overlap (set_overlap), \(H\) is first Lowdin-orthogonalized, \(S^{-1/2}HS^{-1/2}\), as by the topology tools (exact derivatives of \(S^{-1/2}\) included).

Parameters:

  • e_fermi – Real number, or array of real numbers. Fermi energies (all of them are computed from one diagonalization of the mesh).

  • temperature – Positive real or zero. Default value 0. In energy units (\(k_B = 1\)).

  • nk – Positive integer, or tuple (two integers for a plane, three for the full 3D conductivity). Default value 60. k-mesh.

  • plane – Tuple of two integers. Default value (0, 1). 3D only: the reciprocal vectors spanning the plane (see berry_curvature).

  • k_fixed – Real number or None. Default value None. 3D only: the fractional coordinate of the plane along the remaining reciprocal vector; None for the full 3D conductivity. Ignored in 2D.

  • positions – Boolean. Default value True. Include the orbital positions in the bond vectors (see above).

  • refine – Positive integer. Default value 1 (no refinement). Submesh points per direction in the refined cells.

  • refine_fraction – Real in (0, 1]. Default value 0.05. Fraction of the mesh cells that are refined.

Returns:

  • sigma – Real number (or ndarray shaped like e_fermi); in 3D with k_fixed=None, ndarray of shape (3,) (or e_fermi.shape + (3,)).

Example usage:

e_f = np.linspace(-3., 3., 301)
sigma = hal.hall_conductivity(e_f, nk=120)  # plateau at C in the gap
spin_hall_conductivity(e_fermi: float | ArrayLike, temperature: float = 0.0, nk: int | tuple[int, int] = 60, plane: tuple[int, int] = (0, 1), k_fixed: float | None = None, positions: bool = True, spin_axis: str = 'z', refine: int = 1, refine_fraction: float = 0.05) → float | NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the intrinsic spin Hall conductivity of a spinful model (spin=True): the Kubo formula of hall_conductivity with the charge current along \(x\) replaced by the spin current (Sinova et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 92, 126603 (2004))

\[j^{s}_x = \tfrac12\{s, v_x\}\, ,\qquad s = \tfrac{\hbar}{2}\sigma_{a}\, ,\]

i.e. \(\sigma^{s}_{xy} = \frac{e}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{1}{2\pi}\int d^2k\,F^s\), \(F^s = -\sum_{n\neq m}(f_n-f_m)\,\mathrm{Im}[\langle n|j^s_x|m\rangle\langle m|\partial_yH|n\rangle]/(E_n-E_m)^2\) (\(j^s_x\) with \(s = \sigma_a/2\), in units of \(\hbar\)). The unit is \(e/2\pi\): one \(e/\hbar\) from the electric field, one \(\hbar/2\) from the spin, and \(1/2\pi\) from the Brillouin-zone integral, as for \(e^2/h = (e^2/\hbar)/2\pi\). When \(s_z\) is conserved, the two spins decouple and \(j^s_x = \pm\frac{\hbar}{2}v_x\) in each, so in a gap \(\sigma^s_{xy} = \frac{e}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{C_\uparrow - C_\downarrow}{2}\), \(C_\sigma\) the Chern number of each spin sector (the sign of hall_conductivity and chern_number): \(\pm e/2\pi\) for the Kane-Mele quantum spin Hall insulator (Kane and Mele 2005). Rashba coupling breaks the conservation of \(s_z\), and the value is then no longer quantized (the \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) invariant, see z2_invariant, still is).

Parameters:

  • e_fermi – See hall_conductivity.

  • temperature – See hall_conductivity.

  • nk – Positive integer, or tuple of 2 integers. Default value 60.

  • plane – See hall_conductivity.

  • k_fixed – Real number or None. Default value None. 3D only: the plane (required in 3D, where only planes are computed).

  • positions – Boolean. Default value True. See hall_conductivity.

  • spin_axis – ‘x’, ‘y’ or ‘z’. Default value ‘z’. Spin component \(a\) carried by the current.

  • refine – See hall_conductivity.

  • refine_fraction – See hall_conductivity.

Returns:

  • sigma_s – Real number (or ndarray shaped like e_fermi), in units of \(e/2\pi\).

finite_ham(n_cells: int | tuple[int, ...], periodic: bool = False, sparse: bool = False) → NDArray[complex128] | csr_matrix[source]#

Get the real-space Hamiltonian of a finite sample of \(N_1\times N_2\times\dots\) unit cells of the model – open boundaries (a flake, a finite chain), or periodic ones (a torus). Orbital o of cell \((n_1, n_2, n_3)\) is row \(((n_3 N_2 + n_2) N_1 + n_1)\,\mathrm{norb} + o\).

Parameters:

  • n_cells – Positive integer, or tuple of dim positive integers.

  • periodic – Boolean. Default value False. Periodic boundary conditions (the spectrum is then that of get_bands on the \(N_1\times N_2\times\dots\) k-mesh), else open ones.

  • sparse – Boolean. Default value False. Return a sparse CSR matrix (for large samples, e.g. with tbkit.kpm) instead of a dense array.

Returns:

  • ham – Complex ndarray (or CSR matrix), shape (N*norb, N*norb), N the number of cells.

finite_velocity(n_cells: int | tuple[int, ...], periodic: bool = False, sparse: bool = False) → list[NDArray[complex128] | csr_matrix][source]#

Get the velocity operators \(\mathbf{v} = i[H, \mathbf{r}]\) (\(\hbar = 1\)) of the finite sample of finite_ham, from the Cartesian bond vectors of the hoppings rather than from the site coordinates:

\[(v_\alpha)_{ab} = i\,H_{ab}\,d_\alpha\, ,\qquad \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{R} + \boldsymbol\tau_j - \boldsymbol\tau_i\, ,\]

so that they are well defined on a torus (periodic=True), where the position operator is not: a bond that wraps around the sample keeps its short displacement. They are the real-space counterpart of \(\partial H/\partial\mathbf{k}\) with positions=True (hall_conductivity), and the input of tbkit.kpm.hall_conductivity.

Parameters:

  • n_cells – See finite_ham.

  • periodic – Boolean. Default value False. See finite_ham.

  • sparse – Boolean. Default value False. See finite_ham.

Returns:

  • vel – List of space_dim complex ndarrays (or CSR matrices), shape (N*norb, N*norb): \(v_x, v_y, (v_z)\).

get_ham_beta(beta: complex) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

Get the non-Bloch Hamiltonian of a 1D model, \(H(\beta) = \sum_{n} t(n)\, \beta^{n}\): the Bloch Hamiltonian continued off the unit circle, \(\beta = e^{ik}\) with complex \(k\). On the generalized Brillouin zone (see gbz), its spectrum is the open-chain spectrum of a non-Hermitian chain.

Parameters:

beta – Complex number, nonzero.

Returns:

  • ham – Complex ndarray, shape (norb, norb).

spectral_winding(e_ref: complex = 0.0, nk: int = 400) → float[source]#

Get the spectral winding number of a 1D (non-Hermitian) model about the reference energy \(E_r\),

\[W(E_r) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_0^{2\pi} dk\, \partial_k \ln\det\left[H(k) - E_r\right]\, ,\]

the number of times the periodic-chain spectrum winds around \(E_r\) in the complex plane. \(W \neq 0\) for some \(E_r\) is the criterion for the non-Hermitian skin effect: the open-chain eigenstates then pile up at one end (Okuma, Kawabata, Shiozaki and Sato, Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 086801 (2020)).

Parameters:

  • e_ref – Complex number. Default value 0. Reference energy.

  • nk – Positive integer. Default value 400. k-points.

Returns:

  • W – Real number, close to an integer (it is ill defined if \(E_r\) lies on the periodic spectrum).

gbz(energies: ArrayLike) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

Get the generalized Brillouin zone of a 1D non-Hermitian model (Yao and Wang, Phys. Rev. Lett. 121, 086803 (2018); Yokomizo and Murakami, Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 066404 (2019)): for each energy \(E\), the roots of \(\det[H(\beta)-E] = 0\) sorted by modulus, \(|\beta_1|\le\dots\le|\beta_{p+s}|\) (\(p\) the order of its pole at \(\beta = 0\)), and the middle pair \(\beta_p, \beta_{p+1}\). The open-chain spectrum, in the limit of a long chain, is where \(|\beta_p| = |\beta_{p+1}|\); those \(\beta\) trace the generalized Brillouin zone, on which the non-Bloch bands \(H(\beta)\) (see get_ham_beta) replace the Bloch ones. For a Hermitian model it is the unit circle.

Parameters:

energies – Complex array of energies (e.g. open-chain eigenvalues from finite_ham).

Returns:

  • beta – Complex ndarray, shape (len(energies), 2): \(\beta_p, \beta_{p+1}\).

orbital_positions() → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the positions \(\boldsymbol\tau\) of the orbitals within the unit cell (each site twice, for its two spin components, if spin=True).

Returns:

  • tau – Real ndarray, shape (norb, space_dim).

berry_phase(bands: int | list[int], nk: int = 100, direction: int = 0, k_perp: float | tuple[float, float] | None = None, positions: bool = True) → float[source]#

Get the Berry phase of a group of bands along a closed loop across the Brillouin zone, \(\mathbf{k}\to\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{b}_{direction}\),

\[\gamma = \oint \mathbf{A}\cdot d\mathbf{k} = -\arg\det W\, ,\qquad W = \prod_{m} \langle u(\mathbf{k}_m)|u(\mathbf{k}_{m+1})\rangle\, ,\]

with \(\mathbf{A} = i\langle u|\nabla_{\mathbf{k}}u\rangle\) (the convention of berry_curvature). In 1D it is the Zak phase: its value \(\gamma/2\pi\), modulo 1, is the centre of the band’s Wannier functions in units of \(\mathbf{a}_{direction}\) (the polarization).

Parameters:

  • bands – Band index, or list of band indices.

  • nk – Positive integer. Default value 100. Number of k-points on the loop.

  • direction – Integer. Default value 0. Reciprocal vector the loop follows.

  • k_perp – Real number (2D) or pair of real numbers (3D). Default value None (zero). Fractional coordinates of the loop along the other reciprocal vectors.

  • positions – Boolean. Default value True. Include the orbital positions in the Bloch functions (the physical choice: the phase then locates the Wannier centres in the crystal). If False, all orbitals are placed on the cell origin (the periodic gauge of get_ham); the two differ by \(\sum_n\mathbf{b}\cdot\boldsymbol\tau\) weighted by the orbital content, and agree on quantized differences between phases.

Returns:

  • gamma – Real number in \((-\pi, \pi]\).

wannier_centers(bands: int | list[int], nk: int = 100, direction: int = 0, k_perp: float | tuple[float, float] | None = None, positions: bool = True) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the (hybrid) Wannier centres of a group of bands: minus the phases of the eigenvalues of the Wilson loop (see berry_phase), divided by \(2\pi\). They are the positions, in units of \(\mathbf{a}_{direction}\) and modulo 1, of the maximally localized Wannier functions along that direction (hybrid: still Bloch waves along the others, at k_perp). Their sum is \(\gamma/2\pi\), modulo 1.

Parameters:

  • bands – Band index, or list of band indices.

  • nk – Positive integer. Default value 100. Number of k-points on the loop.

  • direction – Integer. Default value 0.

  • k_perp – See berry_phase.

  • positions – Boolean. Default value True. See berry_phase.

Returns:

  • centers – Real ndarray, sorted, in \([0, 1)\).

wannier_flow(bands: int | list[int], nk: int = 100, nk_perp: int = 51, direction: int = 0, flow: int | None = None, k_fixed: float = 0.0, positions: bool = True, k_range: tuple[float, float] = (0.0, 1.0)) → tuple[NDArray[float64], NDArray[float64]][source]#

Get the flow of the hybrid Wannier centres (see wannier_centers) along direction, as the loop is moved across the Brillouin zone along the reciprocal vector flow. In a Chern insulator the centres wind by \(C\) cells over a full period; in a \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) topological insulator, the Kramers pairs swap partners over half a period (see z2_invariant).

Parameters:

  • bands – Band index, or list of band indices.

  • nk – Positive integer. Default value 100. k-points on each loop.

  • nk_perp – Positive integer. Default value 51. Number of loops.

  • direction – Integer. Default value 0. Direction of the loops.

  • flow – Integer. Default value None (the first other direction). Reciprocal vector along which the loops are moved.

  • k_fixed – Real number. Default value 0. 3D only: fractional coordinate along the remaining reciprocal vector.

  • positions – Boolean. Default value True. See berry_phase.

  • k_range – Pair of real numbers. Default value (0, 1). Range of the fractional coordinate along flow (both ends included).

Returns:

  • fracs – Real ndarray, shape (nk_perp,). Fractional coordinates along flow.

  • centers – Real ndarray, shape (nk_perp, len(bands)). Sorted centres, in [0, 1).

z2_invariant(bands: list[int], nk: int = 100, nk_perp: int = 51, direction: int = 0, flow: int | None = None, k_fixed: float = 0.0) → int[source]#

Get the \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) invariant of a time-reversal-symmetric group of bands (an even number, e.g. all occupied bands of the Kane-Mele model) from the flow of its hybrid Wannier centres over half the Brillouin zone (Soluyanov and Vanderbilt, Phys. Rev. B 83, 235401 (2011); Yu, Qi, Bernevig, Fang and Dai, Phys. Rev. B 84, 075119 (2011)): follow the midpoint of the largest gap between the centres, and count, modulo 2, how many centres it jumps over. It is odd when the Kramers partners exchange along the flow – a topological insulator – and even otherwise.

Unlike the parity criterion (parity_z2), it needs no inversion symmetry, so it also works with Rashba coupling.

Parameters:

  • bands – List of band indices (an even number of bands).

  • nk – Positive integer. Default value 100. k-points on each loop.

  • nk_perp – Positive integer. Default value 51. Number of loops over the half zone (the flow must be resolved finely enough that no two centres cross between neighbouring loops unnoticed).

  • direction – Integer. Default value 0. See wannier_flow.

  • flow – Integer. Default value None. See wannier_flow.

  • k_fixed – Real number. Default value 0. 3D only: a time-reversal invariant plane has k_fixed 0 or 0.5 (the weak and strong indices follow from the six such planes).

Returns:

  • nu – 0 (trivial) or 1 (topological).

parity_z2(inversion, bands: list[int]) → int[source]#

Get the \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) invariant of an inversion- and time-reversal-symmetric model from the parity eigenvalues of its occupied bands at the time-reversal-invariant momenta \(\Gamma_i\) (Fu and Kane, Phys. Rev. B 76, 045302 (2007)):

\[(-1)^\nu = \prod_i \delta_i\, ,\qquad \delta_i = \prod_{m=1}^{N} \xi_{2m}(\Gamma_i)\, ,\]

one parity \(\xi = \pm1\) per Kramers pair. In 3D, \(\nu\) is the strong index.

Parameters:

  • inversion – Complex ndarray, shape (norb, norb), or callable of k returning one: the inversion operator \(P\), with \(P H(\mathbf{k}) P^{-1} = H(-\mathbf{k})\) (e.g. swapping the two sublattices of graphene, and the identity on spin).

  • bands – List of band indices (the occupied Kramers pairs).

Returns:

  • nu – 0 (trivial) or 1 (topological).

symmetry_error(op, k_map: str = 'minus', antiunitary: bool = False, anti: bool = False, nk: int = 5, seed: int = 0) → float[source]#

Check a symmetry of the Bloch Hamiltonian,

\[H(g\mathbf{k}) = \pm\, U\, \mathcal{K}H(\mathbf{k})\mathcal{K}^{-1} U^\dagger\, ,\]

with \(g\mathbf{k} = -\mathbf{k}\) or \(\mathbf{k}\), \(\mathcal{K}\) complex conjugation if antiunitary, and the minus sign if anti: time reversal is antiunitary with \(\mathbf{k}\to-\mathbf{k}\) and the plus sign, particle-hole antiunitary with \(\mathbf{k}\to-\mathbf{k}\) and the minus sign, chiral unitary with \(\mathbf{k}\to\mathbf{k}\) and the minus sign, inversion unitary with \(\mathbf{k}\to-\mathbf{k}\) and the plus sign.

Parameters:

  • op – Complex ndarray, shape (norb, norb), or callable of k: \(U\).

  • k_map – ‘minus’ or ‘identity’. Default value ‘minus’.

  • antiunitary – Boolean. Default value False.

  • anti – Boolean. Default value False.

  • nk – Positive integer. Default value 5. Points per direction of the (randomly shifted) test mesh.

  • seed – Integer. Default value 0. Seed of the random shift.

Returns:

  • error – Real number. Largest deviation over the mesh (0 for a symmetry).

tenfold_class(time_reversal=None, particle_hole=None, chiral=None, nk: int = 5, tol: float = 1e-08) → str[source]#

Get the Altland-Zirnbauer symmetry class (the “tenfold way”) of the model from its time-reversal \(T = U_T\mathcal{K}\), particle-hole \(C = U_C\mathcal{K}\) and chiral \(S = U_S\) symmetries. Each given operator is first checked (see symmetry_error) to be a symmetry; the class then follows from \(T^2 = U_TU_T^* = \pm1\), \(C^2 = \pm1\), and the presence of \(S\). Any two of the three imply the third (\(S = TC\)), which need not be given.

Parameters:

  • time_reversal – Matrix \(U_T\), or None (absent).

  • particle_hole – Matrix \(U_C\), or None (absent).

  • chiral – Matrix \(U_S\), or None (absent).

  • nk – Positive integer. Default value 5. See symmetry_error.

  • tol – Positive real. Default value 1e-8. Tolerance of the checks.

Returns:

  • name – String: ‘A’, ‘AIII’, ‘AI’, ‘BDI’, ‘D’, ‘DIII’, ‘AII’, ‘CII’, ‘C’ or ‘CI’.

quantum_geometric_tensor(bands: int | list[int], k: ArrayLike, dk: float = 0.0001, positions: bool = True) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

Get the quantum geometric tensor of a group of bands at \(\mathbf{k}\),

\[Q_{\mu\nu} = \mathrm{Tr}\left[P\,\partial_\mu P\,\partial_\nu P\right] = \sum_{n\in\mathrm{bands}}\langle\partial_\mu u_n|(1-P)|\partial_\nu u_n\rangle\, ,\]

with \(P(\mathbf{k})\) the projector on the bands (gauge invariant, so degeneracies within the group are harmless). Its real part is the quantum metric \(g_{\mu\nu}\) (Provost and Vallee, 1980), minus twice its imaginary part the Berry curvature \(\Omega_{\mu\nu} = -2\,\mathrm{Im}\,Q_{\mu\nu}\) (the convention of berry_curvature, per unit k-area here). They obey \(\sqrt{\det g} \ge |\Omega_{xy}|/2\) in 2D.

Parameters:

  • bands – Band index, or list of band indices.

  • k – k point (see get_ham).

  • dk – Positive real. Default value 1e-4. Finite-difference step.

  • positions – Boolean. Default value True. Include the orbital positions in the Bloch functions. The local metric and curvature depend on this choice (the Berry curvature of berry_curvature is that of positions=False); integrals such as the Chern number do not.

Returns:

  • Q – Complex ndarray, shape (dim, dim), in the k coordinates of get_ham.

plot_dos(nk: int | tuple[int, int] = 30, broadening: float = 0.05, kernel: str = 'gaussian', e_grid: ArrayLike | None = None, fs: float = 20, lw: float = 2.0, figsize: tuple[float, float] | None = None) → Figure[source]#

Plot the (broadened) density of states, obtained by diagonalizing \(H(\mathbf{k})\) over a uniform Brillouin-zone mesh – see tbkit.dos.density_of_states.

Parameters:

  • nk – Positive integer, or tuple of dim positive integers. Default value 30. Number of k-points along each reciprocal lattice vector.

  • broadening – Positive real number. Default value 0.05. Kernel width.

  • kernel – String. Default value ‘gaussian’. ‘gaussian’ or ‘lorentzian’.

  • e_grid – Real ndarray. Default value None. Energies at which to evaluate the density of states.

  • fs – Positive number. Default value 20. Fontsize.

  • lw – Positive number. Default value 2. Linewidth.

  • figsize – Tuple. Default value None. Figure size.

Returns:

  • fig – Figure.

plot_bands(node_labels: list[str] | None = None, fs: float = 20, lw: float = 2.0, ms: float = 0.0, c: str = 'b', lims: tuple[float, float] | None = None, figsize: tuple[float, float] | None = None) → Figure[source]#

Plot the band structure computed by k_path or get_bands, against the cumulative distance along the k-points (vertical lines mark the nodes of a k_path). For a non-Hermitian model, the real part of the energies is plotted.

Parameters:

  • node_labels – List of strings. Default value None. Labels of the high-symmetry points passed to k_path.

  • fs – Positive number. Default value 20. Fontsize.

  • lw – Positive number. Default value 2. Linewidth.

  • ms – Positive number. Default value 0. Marker size.

  • c – Default value ‘b’. Line color.

  • lims – List. Default value None. Energy plot limits.

  • figsize – Tuple. Default value None. Figure size.

Returns:

  • fig – Figure.

show() → None[source]#

Emulate Matplotlib method plt.show().

tbkit.kspace.ribbon(lat: Lattice, list_hop: list[dict], width: int, direction: int = 1, onsite: dict | None = None, spin: bool = False) → KSpace[source]#

Cut a ribbon out of a 2D periodic model: periodic along one primitive vector, finite (open boundary, width unit cells) along the other. This is the standard way to see edge states in a band structure (e.g. the zero-energy edge band of a zigzag graphene ribbon, or the helical edge states of a Kane-Mele ribbon). Cut out of a 3D model, it gives a slab: periodic along the two other primitive vectors, the way to see surface states (e.g. the Fermi arcs of a Weyl semimetal).

Parameters:

  • lat – Lattice class instance (2D or 3D, i.e. two or three primitive vectors). Only unit_cell and prim_vec are used.

  • list_hop – List of dictionaries, in the same format passed to KSpace.set_hopping – the hoppings of the periodic (2D) model that the ribbon is cut from.

  • width – Positive integer. Number of unit cells across the ribbon.

  • direction – 0 or 1 (or 2, in 3D). Default value 1. Which primitive vector (lat.prim_vec[direction]) becomes finite; the others stay periodic.

  • onsite – Dictionary. Default value None. Onsite energies, in the same format passed to KSpace.set_onsite – applied identically on every row of the ribbon.

  • spin – Boolean. Default value False. See KSpace.

Returns:

  • rib – KSpace instance, 1D-periodic (2D-periodic for a slab), with width * len(lat.unit_cell) sites (each site of lat, repeated once per row across the ribbon; row w’s copy of site i is orbital w*len(lat.unit_cell) + i).

Example usage:

# zigzag graphene ribbon, 20 unit cells wide
list_hop = [{'i': 0, 'j': 1, 'R': (0, 0), 't': 1.},
                  {'i': 0, 'j': 1, 'R': (-1, 0), 't': 1.},
                  {'i': 0, 'j': 1, 'R': (0, -1), 't': 1.}]
rib = ribbon(lat, list_hop, width=20)
tbkit.kspace.magnetic_supercell(lat: Lattice, list_hop: list[dict], p: int, q: int, onsite: dict | None = None, spin: bool = False) → KSpace[source]#

Thread a uniform magnetic field through a 2D periodic model, with a rational flux \(\alpha = p/q\) flux quanta per unit cell, and return the Bloch Hamiltonian of its magnetic unit cell: q cells along \(\mathbf{a}_1\). Each hopping gets its Peierls phase (see System.set_peierls_phase)

\[\phi_{ij} = \frac{2\pi}{\Phi_0}\int_{\mathbf{r}_i}^{\mathbf{r}_j}\mathbf{A}\cdot d\mathbf{l} = 2\pi\alpha\,\frac{s_{1,i}+s_{1,j}}{2}\,(s_{2,j}-s_{2,i})\]

in the gauge \(\mathbf{A} = \alpha\Phi_0\, s_1\nabla s_2\), with \((s_1, s_2)\) the fractional coordinates of a point along \((\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2)\), periodic along \(\mathbf{a}_2\). A translation by \(q\mathbf{a}_1\) is a symmetry only up to the gauge transformation \(e^{-2\pi i p s_2}\), which the hoppings crossing the magnetic cell boundary carry. The bands of the result are the Hofstadter subbands, and their chern_number the TKNN integers.

Parameters:

  • lat – Lattice class instance, 2D (two primitive vectors in the plane).

  • list_hop – List of dictionaries, the hoppings of the field-free model, in the format of KSpace.set_hopping.

  • p – Integer. Numerator of the flux per unit cell.

  • q – Positive integer. Denominator of the flux per unit cell: the magnetic cell has q unit cells.

  • onsite – Dictionary. Default value None. Onsite energies, in the format of KSpace.set_onsite, applied to every copy.

  • spin – Boolean. Default value False. See KSpace.

Returns:

  • mag – KSpace instance, with q * len(lat.unit_cell) sites: copy m of site i is site m*len(lat.unit_cell) + i, displaced by \(m\mathbf{a}_1\).

Example usage:

# square lattice, flux 1/3 per plaquette: three Hofstadter bands
mag = magnetic_supercell(lattices.square(), list_hop, p=1, q=3)
chern = [mag.chern_number(bands=[n]) for n in range(3)]

tbkit.lattices module#

A small library of common 2D Bravais lattices, ready to feed into tbkit.lattice.Lattice, tbkit.system.System, or tbkit.kspace.KSpace.

Each function returns a fresh Lattice instance with unit_cell and prim_vec already set (call get_lattice yourself to build a finite flake, or hand it straight to KSpace for a periodic/band-structure calculation). Nearest-neighbor sites are a distance a apart.

Example usage:

import tbkit.lattices as lattices
lat = lattices.kagome()
lat.get_lattice(n1=6, n2=6)
tbkit.lattices.chain(a: float = 1.0) → Lattice[source]#

1D chain: one site per unit cell.

Parameters:

a – Positive real number. Default value 1. Lattice constant.

tbkit.lattices.square(a: float = 1.0) → Lattice[source]#

Square lattice: one site per unit cell.

Parameters:

a – Positive real number. Default value 1. Lattice constant.

tbkit.lattices.triangular(a: float = 1.0) → Lattice[source]#

Triangular lattice: one site per unit cell.

Parameters:

a – Positive real number. Default value 1. Lattice constant.

tbkit.lattices.honeycomb(a: float = 1.0) → Lattice[source]#

Honeycomb lattice (e.g. graphene): two sites per unit cell, nearest neighbors a distance a apart. See also tbkit.graphene.GrapheneLattice for ready-made finite flakes of various shapes.

Parameters:

a – Positive real number. Default value 1. Nearest-neighbor distance.

tbkit.lattices.kagome(a: float = 1.0) → Lattice[source]#

Kagome lattice: three sites per unit cell (tags ‘a’, ‘b’, ‘c’), arranged as corner-sharing triangles on a triangular Bravais lattice. With uniform nearest-neighbor hopping, this lattice famously has an exactly flat band (at E = -2t for hopping amplitude t).

Parameters:

a – Positive real number. Default value 1. Nearest-neighbor distance.

Example usage (nearest-neighbor hopping, for tbkit.kspace.KSpace):

lat = lattices.kagome()
kag = KSpace(lat)
kag.set_hopping([{'i': 0, 'j': 1, 'R': (0, 0), 't': t},
                        {'i': 0, 'j': 1, 'R': (-1, 0), 't': t},
                        {'i': 0, 'j': 2, 'R': (0, 0), 't': t},
                        {'i': 0, 'j': 2, 'R': (0, -1), 't': t},
                        {'i': 1, 'j': 2, 'R': (0, 0), 't': t},
                        {'i': 1, 'j': 2, 'R': (1, -1), 't': t}])
tbkit.lattices.lieb(a: float = 1.0) → Lattice[source]#

Lieb lattice: three sites per unit cell (tag ‘a’: corner site; tags ‘b’, ‘c’: edge-center sites) on a square Bravais lattice. With uniform nearest-neighbor hopping, this lattice famously has an exactly flat band (at E = 0), squeezed between two dispersive bands.

Parameters:

a – Positive real number. Default value 1. Nearest-neighbor distance.

Example usage (nearest-neighbor hopping, for tbkit.kspace.KSpace):

lat = lattices.lieb()
lb = KSpace(lat)
lb.set_hopping([{'i': 0, 'j': 1, 'R': (0, 0), 't': t},
                       {'i': 0, 'j': 1, 'R': (-1, 0), 't': t},
                       {'i': 0, 'j': 2, 'R': (0, 0), 't': t},
                       {'i': 0, 'j': 2, 'R': (0, -1), 't': t}])

tbkit.dos module#

Density of states from a set of eigenenergies, real-space (tbkit.system.System) or reciprocal-space (tbkit.kspace.KSpace, sampled over a k-mesh).

tbkit.dos.density_of_states(energies: ArrayLike, e_grid: ArrayLike | None = None, broadening: float = 0.05, kernel: str = 'gaussian') → tuple[NDArray[float64], NDArray[float64]][source]#

Get the density of states, broadened by a Gaussian or Lorentzian kernel of width broadening:

\[\rho(E) = \sum_n g(E-E_n)\, ,\quad g(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}\ \text{(gaussian)} \ \text{or}\ g(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}\frac{\sigma}{x^2+\sigma^2}\ \text{(lorentzian)}\]

Each level contributes a kernel of unit area, so \(\int\rho(E)dE\) equals the number of levels in energies, for an e_grid wide enough to contain the tails.

Parameters:

  • energies – Array of (real) eigenenergies. Any shape (e.g. the en attribute of System, or of KSpace after get_bands over a k-mesh – flattened automatically).

  • e_grid – Real ndarray. Default value None. Energies at which to evaluate the density of states. If None, a grid of 401 points spanning [min(energies)-3*broadening, max(energies)+3*broadening] is used.

  • broadening – Positive real number. Default value 0.05. Kernel width \(\sigma\).

  • kernel – String. Default value ‘gaussian’. ‘gaussian’ or ‘lorentzian’.

Returns:

  • e_grid – Real ndarray. The energy grid used.

  • dos – Real ndarray, same shape as e_grid. Density of states.

tbkit.propagation module#

class tbkit.propagation.Propagation(lat: Lattice)[source]#

Bases: object

Get lattice time evolution. The time-dependent Schrodinger equation \(i\,\partial_z\psi = H\psi\) is solved by the Crank-Nicolson method,

\[\psi(z+dz) = \left(1 + \tfrac{i}{2}H\,dz\right)^{-1} \left(1 - \tfrac{i}{2}H\,dz\right)\psi(z)\, ,\]

unitary for a Hermitian \(H\).

Parameters:

lat – lattice class instance.

get_propagation(ham: spmatrix, psi_init: NDArray, steps: int, dz: float, norm: bool = False) → None[source]#

Get the time evolution.

Parameters:

  • ham – sparse.csr_matrix. Tight-Binding Hamiltonian.

  • psi_init – np.ndarray. Initial state.

  • steps – Positive Integer. Number of steps.

  • dz – Positive number. Step.

  • norm – Boolean. Default value False. Renormalize the state to \(\sum_i|\psi_i|^2 = 1\) at each step. The Crank-Nicolson step is unitary, so this only matters for a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian (gain/loss), where the norm is not conserved.

get_pumping(hams: list[spmatrix], psi_init: NDArray, steps: int, dz: float, norm: bool = True) → None[source]#

Get the time evolution with adiabatic pumpings.

Parameters:

  • hams – List of sparse.csr_matrices. Tight-Binding Hamiltonians.

  • psi_init – np.ndarray. Initial state.

  • steps – Positive integer. Number of steps.

  • dz – Positive number. Step.

  • norm – Boolean. Default value True. Renormalize the state to \(\sum_i|\psi_i|^2 = 1\) at each step.

The steps are split into len(hams) + 1 equal stages: evolution under hams[0], then len(hams) - 1 stages each interpolating linearly from hams[j] to hams[j+1], then evolution under hams[-1] for the remaining steps. With fewer than len(hams) + 1 steps the stages are empty: the state evolves under hams[-1] from the first step on.

class tbkit.graphene.GrapheneSystem(lat: Lattice)[source]#

Bases: System

set_hop_linear_strain(t: complex, beta: float) → None[source]#

Set nearest-neighbor hoppings according to a linear triaxial strain:

\[t_{ij} = t\left(1 + \tfrac14\beta\, \hat{\boldsymbol\delta}_{ij}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{ij}\right)\]

with \(\hat{\boldsymbol\delta}_{ij}\) the bond direction (from its ‘b’ site to its ‘a’ site) and \(\mathbf{r}_{ij}\) its midpoint. The strain is measured from the coordinate origin, so centre the flake on it (see lattice.center) before calling this.

Parameters:

  • t – Hopping value without strain.

  • beta – Strength of the strain. See get_beta_lims for the range that keeps every hopping positive.

get_butterfly(t: complex, N: int) → None[source]#

Get the spectrum as a function of the strain beta (see set_hop_linear_strain), stored in sys.butterfly, shape (N, sites), with the strain values in sys.betas.

Parameters:

  • t – Unstrained hopping value.

  • N – Positive integer. Number of strain values between the minimal and maximal strains given by get_beta_lims.

get_beta_lims() → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the extremal strain values keeping every hopping positive.

Under set_hop_linear_strain a bond’s amplitude is \(t(1+\tfrac14\beta s_{ij})\), so it stays positive for every bond iff \(-4/\max_{ij} s_{ij} < \beta < -4/\min_{ij} s_{ij}\).

Returns:

  • beta_lims – Real ndarray of length 2, [beta_min, beta_max] (ascending). A bound is infinite if the corresponding \(s_{ij}\) never takes that sign.

tbkit.occupation module#

Occupation of single-particle states: the Fermi-Dirac distribution and the Fermi level that holds a given number of electrons, at zero or finite temperature. Used by tbkit.system.System (a finite spectrum) and tbkit.kspace.KSpace (a Brillouin-zone mesh, with weights).

Energies and temperatures are in the same units (\(k_B = 1\)). Each state holds one electron: for spin-degenerate levels of a spinless model, count two electrons per level.

tbkit.occupation.fermi_dirac(energies: ArrayLike, mu: float, temperature: float = 0.0) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the Fermi-Dirac occupations

\[f(E) = \frac{1}{e^{(E-\mu)/T} + 1}\, ,\]

the step \(\Theta(\mu - E)\) at \(T = 0\) (with \(f = 1/2\) exactly at \(E = \mu\)).

Parameters:

  • energies – Array of real energies (for complex ones, the real part is used).

  • mu – Real number. Chemical potential.

  • temperature – Positive real number or zero. Default value 0.

Returns:

  • f – Real ndarray, same shape as energies.

tbkit.occupation.fermi_level(energies: ArrayLike, n_electrons: float, temperature: float = 0.0, weights: ArrayLike | None = None) → float[source]#

Get the Fermi level \(\mu\) at which \(\sum_n w_n f(E_n) = N_e\).

At \(T = 0\) with a gap above the last occupied level, \(\mu\) is placed midway in that gap (one unit above the top level if every level is filled); if the last electrons only partly fill a (degenerate) level, \(\mu\) is that level’s energy, where fermi_dirac gives each state \(f = 1/2\) – the electron count is then exact only for a half-filled shell. For partly filled degenerate shells, use a small temperature.

Parameters:

  • energies – Array of real energies, any shape (e.g. System.en, or the bands of KSpace.mesh_bands).

  • n_electrons – Positive real number or zero. Number of electrons \(N_e\) (per unit cell, with the weights of a k-mesh).

  • temperature – Positive real number or zero. Default value 0.

  • weights – Array of positive reals, same shape as energies. Default value None (all 1). Weight of each level (e.g. 1/nk on a k-mesh).

Returns:

  • mu – Real number.

tbkit.transport module#

Quantum transport through a finite Tight-Binding device attached to semi-infinite leads: the Landauer-Buttiker picture, in which the (linear, zero-temperature) conductance between two leads is the transmission probability at the Fermi energy,

\[G = \frac{e^2}{h}\,T(E_F)\, ,\qquad T(E) = \mathrm{Tr}\left[\Gamma_{out}\,G^r\,\Gamma_{in}\,G^a\right]\, ,\]

(the Caroli formula) with \(G^r = [E + i\eta - H - \sum_l\Sigma_l]^{-1}\) the device’s retarded Green’s function, \(\Sigma_l\) the self-energy of lead \(l\) and \(\Gamma_l = i(\Sigma_l - \Sigma_l^\dagger)\).

A lead is a semi-infinite repetition of a unit cell with Hamiltonian \(h_0\), each cell coupled to the next one (away from the device) by \(v\); its surface cell is coupled to some device sites by \(\tau\). Its surface Green’s function comes from the decimation algorithm of Lopez Sancho, Lopez Sancho and Rubio (J. Phys. F 15, 851 (1985)), and \(\Sigma = \tau\, g_s\,\tau^\dagger\).

Example usage:

# a perfect chain of 10 sites between two chain leads: T = 1 in the band
tr = Transport(sys.ham)
h0, v = np.zeros((1, 1)), np.ones((1, 1))
tr.add_lead(h0, v, coupling=np.ones((1, 1)), sites=[0])
tr.add_lead(h0, v, coupling=np.ones((1, 1)), sites=[9])
T = tr.transmission(np.linspace(-1.9, 1.9, 50))
tbkit.transport.surface_green(h0: ArrayLike, v: ArrayLike, energy: float, eta: float = 1e-09, tol: float = 1e-12, max_iter: int = 10000) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

Get the surface Green’s function of a semi-infinite lead: cells \(0, 1, 2, \dots\), with \(H_{nn} = h_0\) and \(H_{n,n+1} = v\), \(H_{n+1,n} = v^\dagger\), by the Lopez Sancho-Rubio decimation (each iteration doubles the number of cells accounted for, so it converges in a few tens of steps inside the bands, as \(\eta\to0^+\)).

Parameters:

  • h0 – Square complex array. Cell Hamiltonian.

  • v – Square complex array, same shape. Coupling of a cell to the next one.

  • energy – Real number. Energy.

  • eta – Positive real. Default value 1e-9. Broadening.

  • tol – Positive real. Default value 1e-12. Convergence threshold on the norm of the renormalized couplings.

  • max_iter – Positive integer. Default value 10000.

Returns:

  • gs – Complex ndarray, same shape as h0: \(g_s = [E+i\eta - h_0 - \Sigma_{bulk}]^{-1}\).

tbkit.transport.lead_from_kspace(ks, direction: int = 1) → tuple[NDArray[complex128], NDArray[complex128]][source]#

Get the cell Hamiltonian \(h_0\) and coupling \(v\) of a lead from a 1D periodic model (e.g. a ribbon, see kspace.ribbon), whose hoppings reach at most the neighbouring cells.

Parameters:

  • ks – KSpace instance, 1D.

  • direction – +1 or -1. Default value 1. Direction, along the model’s primitive vector, in which the lead extends away from the device: \(v\) gathers the hoppings to the cell at \(\mathbf{R} = \pm\mathbf{a}_1\).

Returns:

  • h0 – Complex ndarray, shape (norb, norb).

  • v – Complex ndarray, shape (norb, norb).

self_energy(lead: int, energy: float, eta: float = 1e-09) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

tbkit.kpm module#

The kernel polynomial method (KPM; Silver and Roder 1994, Weisse, Wellein, Alvermann and Fehske, Rev. Mod. Phys. 78, 275 (2006)): spectral quantities of a large sparse Hamiltonian from its Chebyshev moments, without diagonalizing it. The spectrum is first mapped into \((-1, 1)\), \(\tilde H = (H - b)/a\); then

\[\delta(E - H) = \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} c_m(E)\, T_m(\tilde H)\, ,\qquad c_m(E) = \frac{(2-\delta_{m0})\,g_m\,T_m(\epsilon)}{a\pi\sqrt{1-\epsilon^2}}\, ,\]

with \(\epsilon = (E-b)/a\), \(T_m\) the Chebyshev polynomials (computed by the recursion \(T_{m+1}(\tilde H)|r\rangle = 2\tilde H\,T_m(\tilde H)|r\rangle - T_{m-1}(\tilde H)|r\rangle\), one sparse matrix-vector product each), and \(g_m\) a kernel that damps the Gibbs oscillations of the truncated series (Jackson: an almost Gaussian broadening of width about \(\pi a/M\)). Traces are estimated with a few random-phase vectors, \(\mathrm{Tr}\,A \approx \frac1R\sum_r\langle r|A|r\rangle\), whose error falls as \(1/\sqrt{RN}\): the cost is \(O(MRN)\) for \(N\) sites, so millions of sites are within reach.

The Hamiltonian must be Hermitian (System.ham, a sparse matrix).

tbkit.kpm.spectral_bounds(ham) → tuple[float, float][source]#

Get bounds on the spectrum of a Hermitian matrix from Gershgorin’s circle theorem: every eigenvalue lies within \(H_{ii} \pm \sum_{j\neq i}|H_{ij}|\) for some \(i\).

Parameters:

ham – Square sparse (or dense) Hermitian matrix.

Returns:

  • e_min, e_max – Real numbers.

tbkit.kpm.jackson_kernel(n_moments: int) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the Jackson kernel

\[g_m = \frac{(M-m+1)\cos\frac{\pi m}{M+1} + \sin\frac{\pi m}{M+1}\cot\frac{\pi}{M+1}}{M+1}\, ,\]

the optimal choice for spectral densities (positive, and resolution about \(\pi/M\) in the scaled energy).

Parameters:

n_moments – Positive integer \(M\).

Returns:

  • g – Real ndarray, shape (n_moments,).

tbkit.kpm.lorentz_kernel(n_moments: int, lam: float = 4.0) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the Lorentz kernel \(g_m = \sinh[\lambda(1 - m/M)]/\sinh\lambda\), which gives Lorentzian broadening (the better choice for Green’s functions).

Parameters:

  • n_moments – Positive integer \(M\).

  • lam – Positive real. Default value 4.

Returns:

  • g – Real ndarray, shape (n_moments,).

tbkit.kpm.dos(ham, n_moments: int = 256, n_random: int | None = 10, e_grid: ArrayLike | None = None, kernel: str = 'jackson', seed=None, bounds: tuple[float, float] | None = None) → tuple[NDArray[float64], NDArray[float64]][source]#

  • n_moments – Positive integer. Default value 256. Number of Chebyshev moments (the energy resolution is about \(\pi a/M\), \(2a\) the spectral width).

  • n_random – Positive integer, or None. Default value 10. Number of random vectors for the trace; None for the exact trace (N vectors: small systems only).

  • e_grid – Real array. Default value None: 1001 Chebyshev nodes over the spectrum. Energies, inside the spectral bounds.

  • kernel – String. Default value ‘jackson’. ‘jackson’ or ‘lorentz’.

  • seed – Default value None. Seed of the random vectors.

Get the KPM density of states of a known spectrum: every level broadened by exactly the truncated, kernel-damped Chebyshev series that dos uses. It is the reference dos converges to (up to the random trace), e.g. for the bands of a periodic model on a k-mesh.

Parameters:

  • site – Integer. Site (row) index.

  • n_moments – Positive integer. Default value 256.
