tbkit.kpm.conductivity(ham, x: ArrayLike, n_moments: int = 128, n_random: int | None = 10, e_grid: ArrayLike | None = None, kernel: str = 'jackson', seed=None, bounds: tuple[float, float] | None = None, area: float | None = None) → tuple[NDArray[float64], NDArray[float64]][source]#

Get the zero-temperature DC conductivity along \(x\) from the Kubo-Greenwood formula,

\[\sigma_{xx}(E) = \frac{\pi}{\Omega}\, \mathrm{Tr}\left[v_x\,\delta(E-H)\,v_x\,\delta(E-H)\right]\, ,\qquad v_x = i[H, x]\, ,\]

in units of \(e^2/\hbar\) (\(\hbar = e = 1\)), by the two-dimensional Chebyshev expansion of Weisse et al. (the moments \(\mu_{mn} = \mathrm{Tr}[v_x T_m(\tilde H) v_x T_n(\tilde H)]\), \(O(M N)\) memory, the DOS needing only \(O(N)\)).

Parameters:

  • ham – Square sparse Hermitian matrix.

  • x – Real array, one coordinate per site (e.g. lat.coor[‘x’]).

  • n_moments – Positive integer. Default value 128.

  • n_random – Positive integer, or None. Default value 10. See dos.

  • e_grid – See dos.

  • kernel – See dos.

  • seed – See dos.

  • bounds – See dos.

  • area – Positive real. Default value None (the number of sites): the area (volume) \(\Omega\) of the sample.

Returns:

  • e_grid – Real ndarray.

  • sigma – Real ndarray, same shape.

tbkit.kpm.hall_conductivity(ham, vx, vy, n_moments: int = 256, n_random: int | None = 10, e_grid: ArrayLike | None = None, kernel: str = 'jackson', seed=None, bounds: tuple[float, float] | None = None, area: float | None = None, temperature: float = 0.0) → tuple[NDArray[float64], NDArray[float64]][source]#

Get the Hall conductivity \(\sigma_{xy}(\mu)\) of a large sample, at any Fermi level and temperature, from the Kubo-Bastin formula expanded in Chebyshev polynomials (Garcia, Covaci and Rappoport, Phys. Rev. Lett. 114, 116602 (2015), Eqs. (1)-(5)). Bastin’s formula,

\[\sigma^{B}_{\alpha\beta}(\mu) = \frac{ie^2\hbar}{\Omega}\int d\varepsilon\,f(\varepsilon)\, \mathrm{Tr}\left[v_\alpha\,\delta(\varepsilon-H)\,v_\beta\,\frac{dG^+}{d\varepsilon} - v_\alpha\,\frac{dG^-}{d\varepsilon}\,v_\beta\,\delta(\varepsilon-H)\right]\, ,\]

\(G^\pm = (\varepsilon - H \pm i0)^{-1}\), becomes, with the spectrum rescaled into \((-1, 1)\), \(\tilde H = (H-b)/a\),

\[\sigma^{B}_{\alpha\beta}(\mu) = \frac{4e^2\hbar}{\pi\Omega a^2}\int_{-1}^{1} d\tilde\varepsilon\,\frac{f(\tilde\varepsilon)}{(1-\tilde\varepsilon^2)^2} \sum_{m,n}\Gamma_{nm}(\tilde\varepsilon)\,\mu^{\alpha\beta}_{nm}\, ,\]
\[\mu^{\alpha\beta}_{mn} = \frac{g_mg_n}{(1+\delta_{m0})(1+\delta_{n0})} \mathrm{Tr}\left[v_\alpha T_m(\tilde H)\,v_\beta T_n(\tilde H)\right]\, ,\]
\[\Gamma_{mn}(\tilde\varepsilon) = (\tilde\varepsilon - in\sqrt{1-\tilde\varepsilon^2})\, e^{in\theta}\,T_m(\tilde\varepsilon) + (\tilde\varepsilon + im\sqrt{1-\tilde\varepsilon^2})\,e^{-im\theta}\,T_n(\tilde\varepsilon)\, ,\]

\(\theta = \arccos\tilde\varepsilon\), \(g_m\) the kernel. The moments \(\mu_{mn}\) (the expensive part: \(5MR\) sparse products, \(O(MN)\) memory) serve every Fermi level and temperature. The energy integral runs over \(|\tilde\varepsilon|\le 0.995\) (the spectrum lies within \(\pm0.99\)): at the ends, \((1-\tilde\varepsilon^2)^{-2}\) would only amplify rounding errors.

Hall part. The value is computed from the antisymmetric moments \((\mu^{xy}_{mn} - \mu^{yx}_{mn})/2\), i.e. it is the Hall conductivity proper, \((\sigma^B_{xy} - \sigma^B_{yx})/2\), the part that the Berry curvature gives (KSpace.hall_conductivity). The symmetric part \((\sigma^B_{xy} + \sigma^B_{yx})/2\) is a Fermi-surface term, like \(\sigma_{xx}\) (see conductivity): it vanishes by symmetry in many lattices (e.g. with a \(C_3\) axis), but in a clean metal of lower symmetry it grows as the kernel’s broadening \(\pi a/M\) shrinks (the Drude weight), and with random vectors it is the main source of noise. Leaving it out removes that noise too. In a clean metal the random-vector estimate is still noisy inside the bands (increase n_random, or the size of the sample); disorder, which makes the Fermi-surface terms finite, and gaps, where they vanish, are much quieter.

Sign and units. The value returned is \(-(\sigma^B_{xy}-\sigma^B_{yx})/2\) in units of \(e^2/h\) (\(\hbar = e = 1\)), the sign of KSpace.hall_conductivity: \(C\) in the gap of a Chern insulator of Chern number \(C\) (KSpace.chern_number). Bastin’s \(\sigma^B_{xy}\) is the Ohm’s-law tensor, \(j_x = \sigma^B_{xy}E_y\) (see KSpace.hall_conductivity).

Sample. The trace must run over a sample without edges – a torus (KSpace.finite_ham and KSpace.finite_velocity with periodic=True): over a whole open flake, the edge currents cancel the bulk and the trace vanishes in a gap.

Parameters:

  • ham – Square sparse Hermitian matrix.

  • vx – Square sparse (or dense) Hermitian matrix, like ham. Velocity \(v_x = i[H, x]\) (see KSpace.finite_velocity). For a spin Hall conductivity, pass the spin current \(\{s, v_x\}/2\) instead (units \(e/2\pi\), see KSpace.spin_hall_conductivity).

  • vy – Square sparse (or dense) Hermitian matrix. Velocity \(v_y\).

  • n_moments – Positive integer. Default value 256. Number of Chebyshev moments \(M\) (energy resolution about \(\pi a/M\)).

  • n_random – Positive integer, or None. Default value 10. See dos.

  • e_grid – Real array. Default value None: 1001 Chebyshev nodes over the spectrum. Fermi energies \(\mu\).

  • kernel – String. Default value ‘jackson’. See dos.

  • seed – See dos.

  • bounds – See dos.

  • area – Positive real. Default value None (the number of orbitals). Area \(\Omega\) of the sample (e.g. number of cells times the cell area).

  • temperature – Positive real or zero. Default value 0. In energy units.

Returns:

  • e_grid – Real ndarray.

  • sigma – Real ndarray, same shape, in units of \(e^2/h\).

tbkit.slater_koster module#

Slater-Koster two-centre integrals (J. C. Slater and G. F. Koster, Phys. Rev. 94, 1498 (1954)) between s, p and d orbitals.

The matrix element between orbital \(\alpha\) on one atom and orbital \(\beta\) on a neighbour at \(\mathbf{d} = d\,(l, m, n)\) depends only on a handful of bond integrals \(V_{ll'\mu}\) (\(\mu = \sigma, \pi, \delta\): the angular momentum about the bond), through the direction cosines \((l, m, n)\) – e.g.

\[E_{s,x} = l\,V_{sp\sigma}\, ,\qquad E_{x,x} = l^2 V_{pp\sigma} + (1-l^2) V_{pp\pi}\, ,\qquad E_{x,y} = lm\,(V_{pp\sigma} - V_{pp\pi})\, .\]

Rather than tabulating all 81 such formulas, they are generated: in a frame whose z axis lies along the bond, the matrix is diagonal in the angular momentum about the bond, with entries \(V_{ll'\mu}\); rotating the frame onto \(\hat{\mathbf{d}}\) gives every entry, \(E(\hat{\mathbf{d}}) = D_{l}(R)\,E(\hat z)\,D_{l'}(R)^T\), with \(D_1 = R\) for the p orbitals and \(D_2\) its action on the quadratic forms of the d orbitals. This is exactly the Slater-Koster table (checked against it in the tests), in the usual real-orbital basis:

's', 'px', 'py', 'pz', 'dxy', 'dyz', 'dzx', 'dx2-y2', 'dz2'.

Bond integrals are given as a dictionary, with keys 'ss_sigma', 'sp_sigma', 'pp_sigma', 'pp_pi', 'sd_sigma', 'pd_sigma', 'pd_pi', 'dd_sigma', 'dd_pi', 'dd_delta' (missing keys are zero). Between different atoms, \(V_{sp\sigma}\) (s on the first atom, p on the second) and \(V_{ps\sigma}\) (p on the first, s on the second) differ: give 'ps_sigma', 'ds_sigma', 'dp_sigma', 'dp_pi' for the latter (they default to their homonuclear counterparts).

tbkit.slater_koster.ORBITALS = {'dx2-y2': 2, 'dxy': 2, 'dyz': 2, 'dz2': 2, 'dzx': 2, 'px': 1, 'py': 1, 'pz': 1, 's': 0}#

Real orbitals, with their angular momentum l.

tbkit.slater_koster.PARAMS = ('ss_sigma', 'sp_sigma', 'ps_sigma', 'pp_sigma', 'pp_pi', 'sd_sigma', 'ds_sigma', 'pd_sigma', 'pd_pi', 'dp_sigma', 'dp_pi', 'dd_sigma', 'dd_pi', 'dd_delta')#

Bond-integral keys (the heteronuclear ps/ds/dp keys are optional).

tbkit.slater_koster.sk_kspace(lat, orbitals: dict[str, list[str]], bonds: dict[int, dict], onsite: dict | None = None, overlap: dict[int, dict] | None = None)[source]#

Get the Slater-Koster Bloch Hamiltonian of a periodic lattice: a KSpace with one orbital per (site, orbital) of the unit cell, and the hoppings of sk_block between the n-th neighbours listed in bonds – the reciprocal-space twin of tbkit.orbital.OrbitalSystem.set_slater_koster().

Returns:

tbkit.orbital module#

Real-space Tight-Binding models with several orbitals per site and an optional spin: OrbitalSystem extends tbkit.system.System with Slater-Koster hoppings between s, p and d orbitals (see tbkit.slater_koster), non-orthogonal bases (an overlap matrix), and spin-dependent terms – Kane-Mele intrinsic spin-orbit coupling, Rashba coupling, Zeeman fields and atomic \(\lambda\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{S}\).

Rows of the Hamiltonian are ordered site by site, then orbital by orbital (in the order given for the site’s tag), then spin (up, down): the row of orbital o with spin s on site i is sys.row(i, o, s).

class tbkit.orbital.OrbitalSystem(lat: Lattice, orbitals: dict[str, list[str]] | None = None, spin: bool = False)[source]#

Bases: System

Solve a real-space Tight-Binding model with several orbitals per site and, optionally, spin.

Parameters:

  • lat – Lattice class instance.

  • orbitals – Dictionary. Default value None (one ‘s’ orbital per site). key: sublattice tag, val: list of orbital names (see tbkit.slater_koster.ORBITALS), e.g. {'a': ['s', 'px', 'py', 'pz']}.

  • spin – Boolean. Default value False. Give every orbital a spin-1/2 degree of freedom.

Everything of System still applies: set_hopping (and the disorder, defect and Peierls methods) sets hoppings \(t\) that connect equal orbitals and equal spins of the two sites (\(t\,\mathbb{1}\)), and set_onsite with plain numbers shifts every orbital of a site. Onsite energies can also be given orbital by orbital, and full hopping blocks come from set_slater_koster, set_spin_orbit, set_rashba or set_hopping_block. Call set_peierls_phase / set_magnetic_field last: they multiply every hopping (and block) set so far.

Example usage:

# graphene's sp3 bands: four orbitals per carbon
sys = OrbitalSystem(lat, orbitals={'a': ['s', 'px', 'py', 'pz'],
                                                'b': ['s', 'px', 'py', 'pz']})
sys.set_onsite({'a': {'s': -8.87}, 'b': {'s': -8.87}})
sys.set_slater_koster(1, {'ss_sigma': -6.77, 'sp_sigma': 5.58,
                                     'pp_sigma': 5.04, 'pp_pi': -3.03})
sys.get_ham()
row(site: int, orbital: str, spin: int = 0) → int[source]#

Get the row of an orbital.

Parameters:

  • site – Integer. Site index.

  • orbital – String. Orbital name (one of the site’s).

  • spin – 0 (up) or 1 (down). Default value 0.

Returns:

  • row – Integer.

set_onsite(dict_onsite: dict) → None[source]#

Set onsite energies.

Parameters:

dict_onsite – Dictionary. key: sublattice tag, val: onsite energy (a number, applied to every orbital of the sites), or a dictionary {orbital: energy} (orbitals not given get 0).

Example usage:

sys.set_onsite({'a': 0.5, 'b': {'s': -8.87, 'pz': 0.}})
set_zeeman(b: tuple[float, float, float]) → None[source]#

Set a Zeeman field \(\mathbf{b}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma\) on every orbital (spin=True only).

Parameters:

b – Tuple of three real numbers \((b_x, b_y, b_z)\).

set_atomic_soc(lam: float, tags: list[str] | None = None) → None[source]#

Set the atomic spin-orbit coupling \(\lambda\,\mathbf{L}\cdot\mathbf{S} = \frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_k L_k\sigma_k\) on the p orbitals (spin=True only; the sites must carry all three of px, py, pz). It splits them into \(j = 3/2\) (at \(+\lambda/2\)) and \(j = 1/2\) (at \(-\lambda\)) levels.

Parameters:

  • lam – Real number. \(\lambda\).

  • tags – List of tags. Default value None (every tag with p orbitals).

set_slater_koster(n: int, params: dict, overlap: dict | None = None) → None[source]#

Set the hoppings between the orbitals of every pair of n-th neighbours from Slater-Koster bond integrals (see tbkit.slater_koster.sk_block()), replacing those set before for the same n. The blocks are spin independent.

Parameters:

  • n – Positive integer. Neighbour order (1 for nearest neighbours).

  • params – Dictionary of bond integrals (e.g. {'pp_sigma': 5.04, 'pp_pi': -3.03}), or dictionary {tag pair: bond integrals} (e.g. {'ab': {...}, 'ba': {...}}, for bonds from an ‘a’ to a ‘b’ site).

  • overlap – Dictionary. Default value None. Bond integrals of the overlap matrix \(S_{ij} = \langle i|j\rangle\), in the same format: the basis is then non-orthogonal, and get_eig solves \(H\psi = ES\psi\).

set_spin_orbit(lam: float, n: int = 2) → None[source]#

Set the Kane-Mele intrinsic spin-orbit coupling on the n-th neighbours (spin=True only),

\[H_{SO} = i\lambda\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}\nu_{ij}\, c_i^\dagger\sigma_z c_j\, ,\qquad \nu_{ij} = \sum_k \mathrm{sign}\left[(\mathbf{d}_{ik}\times\mathbf{d}_{kj})_z\right]\, ,\]

the sum running over the nearest neighbours \(k\) shared by \(i\) and \(j\) (one on the honeycomb lattice, where \(\nu_{ij} = \pm1\) says whether the path turns left or right). It connects equal orbitals of the two sites.

Parameters:

  • lam – Real number. \(\lambda\).

  • n – Positive integer. Default value 2. Neighbour order.

set_rashba(lam: float, n: int = 1) → None[source]#

Set a Rashba spin-orbit coupling on the n-th neighbours (spin=True only), \(H_R = i\lambda\sum_{\langle ij\rangle} c_i^\dagger (\boldsymbol\sigma\times\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{ij})_z\, c_j\), \(\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{ij}\) the bond direction. It connects equal orbitals of the two sites.

Parameters:

  • lam – Real number. \(\lambda\).

  • n – Positive integer. Default value 1.

set_hopping_block(dict_block: dict[tuple[int, int], NDArray]) → None[source]#

Set hopping blocks by hand, added to the others: key: site pair \((i, j)\), val: matrix of shape (rows of i, rows of j) – orbitals, then spin, as row orders them. Their Hermitian conjugates are added.

Parameters:

dict_block – Dictionary.

Clear the hoppings: hop, and every hopping block.

Apply the Peierls substitution (see System.set_peierls_phase) to the hoppings hop and to every hopping block set so far.

Parameters:

phase – Callable phase(xi, yi, xj, yj).

Get the Hamiltonian (and, for a non-orthogonal basis, the overlap matrix overlap).

tbkit.meanfield module#

The Hubbard model in the (collinear, unrestricted Hartree-Fock) mean-field approximation:

\[H = \sum_{ij\sigma} t_{ij}c^\dagger_{i\sigma}c_{j\sigma} + U\sum_i n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow} \;\to\; \sum_\sigma\Big[\sum_{ij} t_{ij}c^\dagger_{i\sigma}c_{j\sigma} + U\sum_i\langle n_{i\bar\sigma}\rangle n_{i\sigma}\Big] - U\sum_i\langle n_{i\uparrow}\rangle\langle n_{i\downarrow}\rangle\, .\]

Each spin moves in the density of the other; the densities are iterated (with linear mixing) until self-consistent. With \(U > 0\) on a bipartite lattice at half filling it reproduces Lieb’s theorem (the total moment \(S = ||A| - |B||/2\)) and the edge magnetism of zigzag graphene.

class tbkit.meanfield.MeanFieldResult(n_up, n_dn, en_up, en_dn, e_fermi, energy, iterations)[source]#

Bases: object

Self-consistent solution of hubbard_mean_field.

Variables:

  • n_up – Real ndarray. Spin-up density on every site.

  • n_dn – Real ndarray. Spin-down density on every site.

  • magnetization – Real ndarray. \(m_i = (n_{i\uparrow} - n_{i\downarrow})/2\).

  • en_up – Real ndarray. Spin-up mean-field energies.

  • en_dn – Real ndarray. Spin-down mean-field energies.

  • e_fermi – Real number. Fermi level.

  • energy – Real number. Mean-field ground-state (free, at T > 0) energy \(\sum f E - U\sum_i n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}\).

  • iterations – Integer. Number of iterations.

property total_spin: float#

Total \(S_z = \sum_i m_i\).

tbkit.meanfield.hubbard_mean_field(ham, U: float | ArrayLike, n_electrons: float, temperature: float = 0.0, n_up: ArrayLike | None = None, n_dn: ArrayLike | None = None, mixing: float = 0.5, tol: float = 1e-08, max_iter: int = 20000, seed=None) → MeanFieldResult[source]#

Solve the Hubbard model in mean field, self-consistently.

The iteration converges to a self-consistent solution, not necessarily the one of lowest energy: compare the energy of the solutions reached from several starts (random seeds, or a staggered magnetization on the two sublattices of a bipartite lattice).

Parameters:

  • ham – Square Hermitian matrix (sparse or dense), the spin-independent single-particle Hamiltonian (e.g. System.ham).

  • U – Real number, or array of one per site. Onsite repulsion.

  • n_electrons – Positive real, at most 2N. Number of electrons (both spins; N for half filling). An integer at T = 0.

  • temperature – Positive real or zero. Default value 0.

  • n_up – Real array. Default value None. Initial spin-up density.

  • n_dn – Real array. Default value None. Initial spin-down density. By default, a small random magnetization on top of the uniform density (to break the spin symmetry).

  • mixing – Real in (0, 1]. Default value 0.5. Fraction of the new density mixed in at each iteration. (Plain linear mixing converges only to stable solutions, but slowly near a magnetic transition: raise max_iter there.)

  • tol – Positive real. Default value 1e-8. Convergence threshold on the largest density change.

  • max_iter – Positive integer. Default value 20000.

  • seed – Default value None. Seed of the random initial magnetization.

Returns:

  • result – MeanFieldResult.

tbkit.exceptional module#

Band touchings of two-dimensional (non-Hermitian) Bloch bands: diabolical points (DPs), Hermitian degeneracies such as graphene’s Dirac points, where two eigenvalues meet but their eigenvectors stay distinct; and exceptional points (EPs), where the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors coalesce, so that \(H(\mathbf{k})\) stops being diagonalizable (a Jordan block).

The tools below tell them apart and compute their invariants. Each takes a model: a 2D KSpace (the plane is the Brillouin zone, in the k coordinates of get_ham), or any callable model(p) returning a square matrix for a point p of a two-parameter plane.

  • Eigenvalue vorticity of a pair of bands around a closed loop \(\Gamma\) (Shen, Zhen and Fu, Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 146402 (2018)),

    \[\nu_{mn}(\Gamma) = -\frac{1}{2\pi}\oint_\Gamma \nabla_{\mathbf{k}}\arg\left[E_m(\mathbf{k}) - E_n(\mathbf{k})\right]\cdot d\mathbf{k}\, .\]

    Band labels are not single-valued around an EP (the two eigenvalues swap after one loop), so vorticity follows the eigenvalues by continuation along the loop (track_eigenvalues), never by sorting. A second-order EP has \(\nu = \pm1/2\), a DP \(\nu = 0\).

  • Discriminant winding (Yang, Schnyder, Hu and Chiu, Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 086401 (2021)): the discriminant \(\Delta(\mathbf{k}) = \prod_{m<n}(E_m - E_n)^2\) is a polynomial in the matrix elements, computed from the characteristic polynomial without any eigenvalue, and its winding \(W(\Gamma) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\oint_\Gamma \nabla_{\mathbf{k}}\arg\Delta\cdot d\mathbf{k}\) counts the EPs inside \(\Gamma\) with their charges. With the two sign conventions above, \(W = -2\sum_{m<n}\nu_{mn}\): \(W = -2\nu = \mp1\) for a second-order EP of a two-band model.

  • EP finder (find_exceptional_points): zeros of \(\Delta\) with \(W \neq 0\) on a plaquette mesh of the Brillouin zone, refined by Newton’s method, with their charge and their order (the size of the Jordan block, from the Petermann factors, which diverge at an EP). Since \(\Delta\) is periodic, the charges sum to zero over the zone: EPs come in pairs of opposite charge (the doubling theorem). When a symmetry makes \(\Delta\) real, EPs form lines instead (exceptional rings, Zhen et al., Nature 525, 354 (2015)), which the finder also returns; fermi_arcs draws the bulk Fermi arcs \(\mathrm{Re}(E_m - E_n) = 0\) that join a pair of EPs (Kozii and Fu, arXiv:1708.05841 (2017); Zhou et al., Science 359, 1009 (2018)).

  • Encircling (encircle): parallel transport of an eigenvector around a loop. Around a DP one loop returns the state with a Berry phase \(\pi\); around a second-order EP one loop swaps the two eigenstates, two loops return the state with a sign flip, and four loops restore it (Heiss, Phys. Rev. E 61, 929 (2000); Dembowski et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 86, 787 (2001)).

tbkit.exceptional.circle(center: ArrayLike, radius: float) → Callable[[float], NDArray[float64]][source]#

Get a circular loop, run counterclockwise: \(\mathbf{k}(s) = \mathbf{k}_0 + r(\cos 2\pi s, \sin 2\pi s)\), \(s\in[0, 1]\).

Parameters:

  • center – Tuple/list/ndarray of 2 real numbers. \(\mathbf{k}_0\).

  • radius – Positive real. \(r\).

Returns:

  • loop – Callable of s, returning a real ndarray of shape (2,).

tbkit.exceptional.track_eigenvalues(model, loop, n_loops: int = 1, nk: int = 100) → tuple[NDArray[float64], NDArray[float64], NDArray[complex128]][source]#

Follow the (complex) eigenvalues of \(H(\mathbf{k})\) continuously around a closed loop, n_loops times. Each step (at most 1/nk of the loop) matches the new eigenvalues to a linear prediction from the previous ones, and is halved while that matching is ambiguous; nothing depends on how the eigensolver orders its output. Label \(m\) is the \(m\)-th eigenvalue at the start of the loop, sorted by real part. After one loop around a second-order exceptional point the labels come back swapped: en[-1] is then a permutation of en[0].

Parameters:

  • model – 2D KSpace, or callable of a point of a plane returning a square matrix.

  • loop – Closed loop: a callable of \(s\in[0, 1]\) returning a point (e.g. circle), or an array of polygon vertices, shape (m, 2). For a KSpace, points are k in the coordinates of get_ham, and a loop may close up to a reciprocal lattice vector.

  • n_loops – Positive integer. Default value 1. Number of turns.

  • nk – Positive integer. Default value 100. Steps per turn before refinement.

Returns:

  • s – Real ndarray, shape (n,). Loop parameter, from 0 to n_loops.

  • k – Real ndarray, shape (n, 2). Points of the loop.

  • en – Complex ndarray, shape (n, norb). Eigenvalues, en[:, m] continuous in s.

tbkit.exceptional.vorticity(model, loop, bands: tuple[int, int] = (0, 1), nk: int = 100) → float[source]#

Get the eigenvalue vorticity of a pair of bands around a closed loop \(\Gamma\) (Shen, Zhen and Fu, Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 146402 (2018)),

\[\nu_{mn}(\Gamma) = -\frac{1}{2\pi}\oint_\Gamma \nabla_{\mathbf{k}}\arg\left[E_m(\mathbf{k}) - E_n(\mathbf{k})\right] \cdot d\mathbf{k}\, ,\]

with the eigenvalues followed by continuation (see track_eigenvalues). \(\nu_{mn} = \pm1/2\) around a second-order exceptional point, where \(E_m - E_n \propto \sqrt{\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{k}_{EP}}\) changes sign after one loop; \(\pm1/3\) for each pair of a third-order one; 0 around a diabolical point, or a loop enclosing no degeneracy. \(\nu_{mn} = \nu_{nm}\).

Parameters:

  • model – See track_eigenvalues.

  • loop – See track_eigenvalues. Counterclockwise for the sign above.

  • bands – Pair of distinct integers. Default value (0, 1). Band labels \((m, n)\) at the start of the loop, sorted by real part.

  • nk – Positive integer. Default value 100. See track_eigenvalues.

Returns:

  • nu – Real number, a multiple of 1/2 around second-order EPs.

tbkit.exceptional.discriminant(model, k: ArrayLike) → complex[source]#

Get the discriminant of \(H(\mathbf{k})\),

\[\Delta(\mathbf{k}) = \prod_{m<n}\left[E_m(\mathbf{k}) - E_n(\mathbf{k})\right]^2 = (-1)^{N(N-1)/2}\,\mathrm{Res}(p, p')\, ,\]

computed as the resultant of the characteristic polynomial \(p(E) = \det[E - H(\mathbf{k})]\) and its derivative (the determinant of their Sylvester matrix), without the eigenvalues. It is a polynomial in the matrix elements, hence smooth and single-valued, and it vanishes exactly where two eigenvalues meet. For a two-band model \(H = d_0 + \mathbf{d}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma\), \(\Delta = 4\,\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{d}\).

Parameters:

  • model – See track_eigenvalues.

  • k – Tuple/list/ndarray of 2 real numbers. Point of the plane.

Returns:

  • delta – Complex number, in units of energy^(N(N-1)) (1 if N = 1).

tbkit.exceptional.discriminant_winding(model, loop, nk: int = 100) → float[source]#

Get the winding number of the discriminant (see discriminant) around a closed loop \(\Gamma\) (Yang, Schnyder, Hu and Chiu, Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 086401 (2021)),

\[W(\Gamma) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\oint_\Gamma \nabla_{\mathbf{k}}\arg\Delta(\mathbf{k}) \cdot d\mathbf{k} = -2\sum_{m<n}\nu_{mn}(\Gamma)\, ,\]

the total charge of the exceptional points inside \(\Gamma\) (\(\pm1\) for a second-order EP, where \(\Delta\) vanishes linearly). It needs no eigenvalue tracking. A diabolical point has \(W = 0\): \(\Delta \geq 0\) for a Hermitian model. The relation to the vorticities vorticity holds with the signs as written, the minus sign coming from Shen, Zhen and Fu’s definition of \(\nu\).

Parameters:

  • model – See track_eigenvalues.

  • loop – See track_eigenvalues. Counterclockwise for the sign above.

  • nk – Positive integer. Default value 100. Points on the loop; a step along which \(\arg\Delta\) turns by more than \(\pi/4\) is bisected.

Returns:

  • W – Real number, close to an integer.

tbkit.exceptional.petermann_factors(model, k: ArrayLike) → tuple[NDArray[complex128], NDArray[float64]][source]#

Get the eigenvalues of \(H(\mathbf{k})\) and their Petermann factors

\[K_n = \frac{\langle L_n|L_n\rangle\langle R_n|R_n\rangle}{|\langle L_n|R_n\rangle|^2} \geq 1\, ,\]

with \(|R_n\rangle\), \(|L_n\rangle\) the right and left eigenvectors: 1 for a normal (e.g. Hermitian) matrix, diverging at an exceptional point, where \(\langle L_n|R_n\rangle \to 0\) (as \(|\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{k}_{EP}|^{-1}\) near a second-order one).

Parameters:

  • model – See track_eigenvalues.

  • k – Tuple/list/ndarray of 2 real numbers.

Returns:

  • en – Complex ndarray, shape (norb,). Eigenvalues, sorted by real part.

  • K – Real ndarray, shape (norb,). Petermann factors.

class tbkit.exceptional.ExceptionalPoints(k, charge, order, petermann, energy, lines)[source]#

Bases: object

Exceptional points of a 2D model, see find_exceptional_points.

Variables:

  • k – Real ndarray, shape (n, 2). Isolated exceptional points.

  • charge – Integer ndarray, shape (n,). Discriminant winding around each one (see discriminant_winding): \(\pm1\) for a second-order EP.

  • order – Integer ndarray, shape (n,). Number of coalescing eigenvalues (the size of the Jordan block): 2, 3, …

  • petermann – Real ndarray, shape (n,). Largest Petermann factor at each point (divergent at an EP: about \(10^{8}\) or more once refined).

  • energy – Complex ndarray, shape (n,). The coalescing eigenvalue.

  • lines – Real ndarray, shape (m, 2). Points on exceptional lines (rings), when a symmetry makes the discriminant real; empty otherwise.

property total_charge: int#

Sum of the charges: zero over a whole Brillouin zone (doubling theorem).

tbkit.exceptional.find_exceptional_points(ks: KSpace, nk: int = 40, tol: float = 1e-12, max_iter: int = 50) → ExceptionalPoints[source]#

Locate the exceptional points of a 2D model over its Brillouin zone.

  1. The discriminant \(\Delta(\mathbf{k})\) (see discriminant) is computed on an \(nk\times nk\) mesh of the zone (shifted off the high-symmetry lines), and its winding around every plaquette from the phase changes along the mesh edges (bisected where \(\arg\Delta\) turns by more than \(\pi/4\)). A plaquette with a nonzero winding \(w\) holds an EP.

  2. Each one is refined by Newton’s method on \((\mathrm{Re}\,\Delta, \mathrm{Im}\,\Delta) = 0\) from the plaquette centre (the step multiplied by \(|w|\), the multiplicity of the zero).

  3. Its charge is the winding of \(\Delta\) around a small circle (a quarter of a plaquette), and its order the number of eigenvalues whose Petermann factor diverges there (see petermann_factors).

If a symmetry makes \(\Delta\) real everywhere (up to a constant phase), EPs are not isolated: they form lines, exceptional rings, where \(\Delta\) changes sign. The lines are then sampled where they cross the mesh edges (bisection to machine precision), and no isolated point is returned. A Hermitian model has \(\Delta \geq 0\), and no EP.

Since \(\Delta\) is periodic, the charges add up to zero (total_charge): EPs come in pairs of opposite charge. The mesh must be fine enough that no plaquette holds two EPs of opposite charge.

Parameters:

  • ks – KSpace instance with two primitive vectors.

  • nk – Positive integer. Default value 40. Mesh points along each reciprocal vector.

  • tol – Positive real. Default value 1e-12. Newton’s method stops when a step is shorter than tol (units of k).

  • max_iter – Positive integer. Default value 50. Newton iterations.

Returns:

  • eps – ExceptionalPoints instance (positions k, charge, order, petermann, energy, and the exceptional lines).

tbkit.exceptional.fermi_arcs(ks: KSpace, nk: int = 60) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the bulk Fermi arcs of a 2D non-Hermitian model: the curves where two eigenvalues have equal real parts but different imaginary parts, \(\mathrm{Re}(E_m - E_n) = 0\), \(\mathrm{Im}(E_m - E_n) \neq 0\). Such an arc joins two exceptional points of opposite charge (for a two-band model it is where \(\Delta\) is real and negative, see discriminant); it is what a Hermitian Dirac point turns into when a non-Hermitian term splits it into an EP pair (Kozii and Fu 2017; Zhou et al., Science 359, 1009 (2018)).

Along every edge of an \(nk\times nk\) mesh of the zone the eigenvalues are followed by continuation (see track_eigenvalues), and where \(\mathrm{Re}(E_m - E_n)\) changes sign, the crossing is found by bisection. Regions where the real parts coincide over an area (inside an exceptional ring) show no sign change and are not reported, and neither are edges that cross an exceptional point or line, along which the eigenvalues cannot be followed.

Parameters:

  • ks – KSpace instance with two primitive vectors.

  • nk – Positive integer. Default value 60. Mesh points along each reciprocal vector.

Returns:

  • points – Real ndarray, shape (m, 2). Points on the arcs.

class tbkit.exceptional.Encircling(s, k, en, vector, band, final_band, overlap)[source]#

Bases: object

An eigenstate carried around a loop by parallel transport, see encircle.

Variables:

  • s – Real ndarray, shape (n,). Loop parameter, from 0 to n_loops.

  • k – Real ndarray, shape (n, 2). Points of the loop.

  • en – Complex ndarray, shape (n, norb). All eigenvalues, followed by continuation (see track_eigenvalues).

  • vector – Complex ndarray, shape (n, norb). The transported right eigenvector \(|R(s)\rangle\) of the followed state.

  • band – Integer. Label of the state at the start.

  • final_band – Integer. Label, at the start, of the eigenvalue the state ends on (different from band after an odd number of loops around a second-order EP: the states swap).

  • overlap – Complex number. \(c = \langle L_{f}(0)|R(\mathrm{end})\rangle\), with \(f\) = final_band and \(\langle L_f(0)|R_f(0)\rangle = 1\): the transported state is \(c\,|R_f(0)\rangle\). If final_band is band, \(c = e^{i\gamma}\) (times a modulus that is 1 for a Hermitian model), \(\gamma\) the geometric phase; otherwise its phase depends on the (arbitrary) phase of \(|R_f(0)\rangle\).

property phase: float#

Accumulated phase \(\arg c\) in \((-\pi, \pi]\) (the Berry phase when the state returns to itself).

tbkit.exceptional.encircle(model, loop, band: int = 0, n_loops: int = 1, nk: int = 100) → Encircling[source]#

Carry an eigenstate around a closed loop n_loops times, by parallel transport of its right eigenvector \(|R\rangle\), with the left one \(\langle L|\) normalized by \(\langle L|R\rangle = 1\):

\[\langle L(\mathbf{k})|\partial_s R(\mathbf{k})\rangle = 0\, ,\]

discretized symmetrically between successive points, \(\langle L_j + L_{j+1}|R_{j+1} - R_j\rangle = 0\) (second order in the step; the eigenvalue is followed by continuation, see track_eigenvalues). For a Hermitian model \(L = R\), the norm is kept exactly, and this is the usual parallel transport: the state comes back as \(e^{i\gamma}|R\rangle\), \(\gamma = \oint i\langle u|\nabla_{\mathbf{k}}u\rangle\cdot d\mathbf{k}\) the Berry phase (the convention of KSpace.berry_phase), \(\pi\) around a diabolical point. Around a second-order exceptional point:

  • one loop swaps the two eigenstates (final_band differs from band);

  • two loops bring the state back with a sign flip, \(\gamma = \pi\);

  • four loops restore it.

Parameters:

  • model – See track_eigenvalues.

  • loop – See track_eigenvalues.

  • band – Integer. Default value 0. Label of the state at the start of the loop (by real part of the eigenvalue).

  • n_loops – Positive integer. Default value 1. Number of turns.

  • nk – Positive integer. Default value 100. Steps per turn before refinement.

Returns:

  • result – Encircling instance (en, the transported vector, final_band, overlap and phase).

tbkit.bdg module#

Superconductivity in the Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) formalism. With a pairing term \(\sum_{ij}\Delta_{ij}c^\dagger_ic^\dagger_j + h.c.\), the Hamiltonian is \(\frac12\Psi^\dagger H_{BdG}\Psi\) in the Nambu basis \(\Psi = (c_1, \dots, c_N, c_1^\dagger, \dots, c_N^\dagger)^T\),

\[\begin{split}H_{BdG} = \begin{pmatrix} h - \mu & \Delta \\ \Delta^\dagger & -(h-\mu)^T \end{pmatrix}\, ,\end{split}\]

with \(\Delta^T = -\Delta\) (Fermi statistics). Its spectrum is symmetric, \(\pm E_n\), by the particle-hole symmetry \(\tau_x H_{BdG}^*\tau_x = -H_{BdG}\); the quasiparticle energies are the \(E_n \ge 0\), and a zero mode is a Majorana mode. Real-space models come from bdg_ham, periodic ones from bdg_kspace (a tbkit.kspace.KSpace with the holes as extra orbitals, so its bands, Berry phases, finite_ham, … all apply).

tbkit.bdg.bdg_ham(ham, pairing, mu: float = 0.0) → csr_matrix[source]#

Get the real-space BdG Hamiltonian (see the module docstring).

Parameters:

  • ham – Square Hermitian matrix, shape (N, N) (e.g. System.ham).

  • pairing – Square antisymmetric matrix, shape (N, N): \(\Delta\) (see pairing_bonds, pairing_s_wave).

  • mu – Real number. Default value 0. Chemical potential.

Returns:

  • ham_bdg – Sparse CSR matrix, shape (2N, 2N).

tbkit.bdg.pairing_bonds(sys, delta: complex) → csr_matrix[source]#

Get a p-wave (odd) pairing on the bonds of sys.hop: \(\Delta_{ij} = \Delta\), \(\Delta_{ji} = -\Delta\) for every stored hopping \(i\to j\) (oriented as System.set_hopping stores them: angle in \([0, 180)\)). On a chain it is Kitaev’s \(\Delta\,c^\dagger_jc^\dagger_{j+1}\).

Parameters:

  • sys – System instance, with hoppings.

  • delta – Complex number. \(\Delta\).

Returns:

  • pairing – Sparse CSR matrix, shape (sites, sites).

tbkit.bdg.pairing_s_wave(n_sites: int, delta: complex) → csr_matrix[source]#

Get an onsite singlet (s-wave) pairing \(\Delta\sum_i c^\dagger_{i\uparrow}c^\dagger_{i\downarrow} + h.c.\) for a spinful model with rows ordered site by site, spin up then down (as KSpace with spin=True and OrbitalSystem with one orbital).

Parameters:

  • n_sites – Positive integer. Number of sites.

  • delta – Complex number. \(\Delta\).

Returns:

  • pairing – Sparse CSR matrix, shape (2 n_sites, 2 n_sites).

tbkit.bdg.bdg_kspace(ks, pairing: list[dict], mu: float = 0.0)[source]#

Get the BdG Bloch Hamiltonian of a periodic model,

\[\begin{split}H_{BdG}(\mathbf{k}) = \begin{pmatrix} h(\mathbf{k})-\mu & \Delta(\mathbf{k}) \\ \Delta(\mathbf{k})^\dagger & -[h(-\mathbf{k})-\mu]^T\end{pmatrix}\, ,\qquad \Delta(\mathbf{k}) = \sum_{\mathbf{R}}\Delta_{ij}(\mathbf{R})\,e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}}\, ,\end{split}\]

as a new KSpace whose orbitals are those of ks (particles, 0 ... norb-1) followed by their holes (norb ... 2 norb-1, at the same positions). Each pairing \(\Delta\,c^\dagger_{i,\mathbf{0}}c^\dagger_{j,\mathbf{R}} + h.c.\) enters antisymmetrized, \(\Delta_{ij}(\mathbf{R}) = -\Delta_{ji}(-\mathbf{R})\).

Parameters:

  • ks – KSpace instance (Hermitian, orthogonal basis).

  • pairing – List of dictionaries with keys (‘i’, ‘j’, ‘R’, ‘delta’): orbital indices of ks (0 ... norb-1; with spin=True, 2*site + spin), lattice vector, amplitude.

  • mu – Real number. Default value 0. Chemical potential.

Returns:

  • ks_bdg – KSpace instance, 2 norb orbitals.

Example usage:

# Kitaev chain: E(k) = +-sqrt((2t cos k - mu)^2 + 4 Delta^2 sin^2 k)
chain = KSpace(lattices.chain())
chain.set_hopping([{'i': 0, 'j': 0, 'R': (1,), 't': t}])
kit = bdg_kspace(chain, [{'i': 0, 'j': 0, 'R': (1,), 'delta': delta}], mu=mu)
tbkit.bdg.particle_hole(n: int) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the unitary part \(\tau_x\) of the BdG particle-hole symmetry \(C = \tau_x\mathcal{K}\) (\(C^2 = +1\)), for n particle orbitals: pass it to KSpace.symmetry_error (antiunitary=True, anti=True) or KSpace.tenfold_class (particle_hole=).

Parameters:

n – Positive integer. Number of particle orbitals.

Returns:

  • tau_x – Real ndarray, shape (2n, 2n).

tbkit.floquet module#

Floquet theory of periodically driven Tight-Binding models, \(H(t + T) = H(t)\), \(\omega = 2\pi/T\) (\(\hbar = 1\)).

The evolution over one period, \(U(T) = \mathcal{T}e^{-i\int_0^TH(t)dt} = e^{-iH_FT}\), defines the Floquet Hamiltonian \(H_F\), whose eigenvalues – the quasienergies \(\epsilon\), defined modulo \(\omega\) – replace the energies of a static model: the driven system, observed once per period, behaves as if it were static with Hamiltonian \(H_F\). Driving can therefore engineer band structures and their topology: circularly polarized light turns graphene into a Chern insulator (Oka and Aoki, Phys. Rev. B 79, 081406 (2009); Kitagawa, Oka, Brataas, Fu and Demler, Phys. Rev. B 84, 235108 (2011)).

Two routes give the quasienergies, checked against each other in the tests:

  • the time-ordered product of short-time propagators (evolution_operator, quasienergies, effective_hamiltonian);

  • the Sambe (extended) space of the harmonics \(H(t) = \sum_m H_m e^{-im\omega t}\), a static eigenvalue problem (harmonics, sambe_hamiltonian).

FloquetKSpace makes a driven KSpace model: its get_ham is the Floquet Hamiltonian \(H_F(\mathbf{k})\), so its bands, Berry curvature and Chern numbers are the driven ones.

Anomalous Floquet phases. The quasienergies are defined modulo \(\omega\), so \(H_F\) depends on where the branch cut of the logarithm is put (the epsilon arguments). The Chern numbers of the Floquet bands no longer count the edge states: every band can have \(C = 0\) while chiral edge states cross every gap (Kitagawa, Berg, Rudner and Demler, Phys. Rev. B 82, 235114 (2010)). The winding number of Rudner, Lindner, Berg and Levin (Phys. Rev. X 3, 031005 (2013)), which uses the evolution at all times of the period, does (DrivenKSpace.winding_number):

  • DrivenKSpace makes a driven Bloch model out of any time-dependent \(H(\mathbf{k}, t)\);

  • step_drive builds a piecewise-constant drive from a list of models (KSpace models, ribbons made by kspace.ribbon, real-space System instances, or matrices), evolved exactly as a product of step exponentials (StepDrive in real space);

  • DrivenKSpace.edge_state_count counts the chiral edge states of a driven ribbon, independently of the bulk winding number.

tbkit.floquet.evolution_operator(ham_t: Callable, period: float, n_steps: int = 100) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

Get the one-period evolution operator \(U(T) = \prod_m e^{-iH(t_m)\,\delta t}\) (later times on the left, midpoints \(t_m = (m + 1/2)\delta t\), error \(O(\delta t^2)\)).

Parameters:

  • ham_t – Callable. ham_t(t) returns the Hamiltonian at time t (a square matrix).

  • period – Positive real. \(T\).

  • n_steps – Positive integer. Default value 100. Time steps per period.

Returns:

  • U – Complex ndarray, the shape of the Hamiltonian.

tbkit.floquet.quasienergies(ham_t: Callable, period: float, n_steps: int = 100, epsilon: float | None = None) → NDArray[float64][source]#

Get the quasienergies \(\epsilon\), eigenvalues of the Floquet Hamiltonian, in the first Floquet zone \([-\omega/2, \omega/2)\), or in \([\epsilon_{cut} - \omega, \epsilon_{cut})\).

Parameters:

  • ham_t – Callable. See evolution_operator.

  • period – Positive real.

  • n_steps – Positive integer. Default value 100.

  • epsilon – Real number. Default value None (the zone \([-\omega/2, \omega/2)\)). Branch cut, see effective_hamiltonian.

Returns:

  • eps – Real ndarray, sorted.

tbkit.floquet.effective_hamiltonian(ham_t: Callable, period: float, n_steps: int = 100, epsilon: float | None = None) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

Get the Floquet Hamiltonian \(H_F = \frac{i}{T}\ln U(T)\), with its quasienergies in the first Floquet zone (Hermitian for a Hermitian drive).

The logarithm is defined up to multiples of \(\omega\) on each eigenvalue: epsilon puts its branch cut at the quasienergy \(\epsilon_{cut}\) (the phase \(e^{-i\epsilon_{cut}T}\) of \(U\)), so that the quasienergies lie in \([\epsilon_{cut} - \omega, \epsilon_{cut})\). The default, the zone \([-\omega/2, \omega/2)\), is the cut \(\epsilon_{cut} = \omega/2\). Rudner et al. (2013) take \((\epsilon_{cut}, \epsilon_{cut} + \omega]\) instead: \(H_F\) shifted by \(\omega\) (the same projectors, so the same Chern numbers and winding numbers).

Parameters:

  • ham_t – Callable. See evolution_operator.

  • period – Positive real.

  • n_steps – Positive integer. Default value 100.

  • epsilon – Real number. Default value None (\(\epsilon_{cut} = \omega/2\), computed exactly as before this option existed). Branch cut, best placed in a quasienergy gap.

Returns:

  • H_F – Complex ndarray.

tbkit.floquet.harmonics(ham_t: Callable, period: float, n_harmonics: int, n_samples: int | None = None) → dict[source]#

Get the Fourier components \(H_m = \frac1T\int_0^T H(t)\,e^{im\omega t}\,dt\) of the drive, \(H(t) = \sum_m H_m e^{-im\omega t}\), for \(|m| \le\) n_harmonics (exact for a drive with no higher harmonics).

Parameters:

  • ham_t – Callable. See evolution_operator.

  • period – Positive real.

  • n_harmonics – Positive integer or zero.

  • n_samples – Positive integer. Default value None (4 n_harmonics + 16). Time samples per period.

Returns:

  • H_m – Dictionary {m: complex ndarray}.

tbkit.floquet.sambe_hamiltonian(harm: dict, omega: float, n_max: int) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

Get the Sambe-space Floquet Hamiltonian, truncated to the photon sectors \(n = -n_{max}, \dots, n_{max}\):

\[(\mathcal{H})_{nn'} = H_{n-n'} + n\omega\,\delta_{nn'}\, .\]

Its eigenvalues are the quasienergies, repeated in every Floquet zone (shifted by multiples of \(\omega\)); those of the central zone converge fastest as n_max grows.

Parameters:

  • harm – Dictionary {m: square complex array}, see harmonics.

  • omega – Positive real. Driving frequency.

  • n_max – Positive integer or zero.

Returns:

  • H – Complex ndarray, shape ((2 n_max + 1) d, (2 n_max + 1) d).

class tbkit.floquet.StepDrive(hams: list, durations: ArrayLike, epsilon: float | None = None)[source]#

Bases: object

A finite (real-space) system driven by a piecewise-constant Hamiltonian: \(H(t) = H_n\) for \(t_{n-1} \le t < t_n = \delta t_1 + \dots + \delta t_n\), repeated with period \(T = \sum_n \delta t_n\). The evolution is exact, a product of step exponentials,

\[U(t) = e^{-iH_n(t - t_{n-1})}\,e^{-iH_{n-1}\delta t_{n-1}}\cdots e^{-iH_1\delta t_1}\, ,\]

with no time grid. Built by step_drive from System instances or matrices (see DrivenKSpace for Bloch models and ribbons).

Parameters:

  • hams – List of square complex ndarrays, one Hermitian matrix per step (all of one shape).

  • durations – List of positive reals, the step durations \(\delta t_n\).

  • epsilon – Real number. Default value None. Default branch cut of quasienergies and effective_hamiltonian.

tbkit.floquet.step_drive(models: list, durations: ArrayLike, epsilon: float | None = None)[source]#

Build a piecewise-constant drive: the Hamiltonian of models[n] acts for durations[n], in order, and the cycle repeats with period \(T = \sum_n \delta t_n\). The evolution is exact (a product of step exponentials, no time grid, see StepDrive).

Parameters:

  • models –

    List of models of one size, all of one kind:

    • KSpace instances (including ribbons made by kspace.ribbon) – returns a DrivenKSpace, whose get_ham is the Floquet Hamiltonian \(H_F(\mathbf{k})\);

    • System instances (their get_ham is called) or square matrices (dense or scipy.sparse) – returns a StepDrive.

    Each must be Hermitian; KSpace models need an orthogonal basis.

  • durations – List of positive reals. \(\delta t_n\), one per model.

  • epsilon – Real number. Default value None. Branch cut of the Floquet Hamiltonian (see effective_hamiltonian).

Returns:

  • drive – DrivenKSpace or StepDrive.

Example usage:

# Rudner et al. (2013): hopping along one bond direction per step
drive = step_drive([ks1, ks2, ks3, ks4, ks5], [T/5] * 5)
w = drive.winding_number(epsilon=np.pi / T)
class tbkit.floquet.DrivenKSpace(ks, ham_kt: Callable, period: float, n_steps: int = 100, epsilon: float | None = None)[source]#

Bases: object

A periodic model driven by any time-periodic Bloch Hamiltonian \(H(\mathbf{k}, t + T) = H(\mathbf{k}, t)\).

It is a copy of the KSpace model whose get_ham returns the Floquet Hamiltonian \(H_F(\mathbf{k}) = \frac{i}{T}\ln U(\mathbf{k}, T)\) (branch cut at epsilon, see effective_hamiltonian), so get_bands, k_path, berry_curvature, chern_number, … describe the driven system, and winding_number gives its anomalous topology. The evolution \(U(\mathbf{k}, T)\) is the product of n_steps midpoint propagators (see evolution_operator); drives built by step_drive are evolved exactly. Real-space methods that need static hoppings (finite_ham, get_ham_beta, gbz) are not available.

Parameters:

  • ks – KSpace instance. The model driven: its lattice, orbitals and k-space conventions (periodic gauge) are those of the driven model.

  • ham_kt – Callable. ham_kt(k, t) returns the Hermitian Bloch Hamiltonian \(H(\mathbf{k}, t)\), shape (norb, norb), in the periodic gauge of ks (\(H(\mathbf{k} + \mathbf{G}, t) = H(\mathbf{k}, t)\)).

  • period – Positive real. \(T\).

  • n_steps – Positive integer. Default value 100. Time steps per period.

  • epsilon – Real number. Default value None (quasienergies in \([-\omega/2, \omega/2)\)). Branch cut of get_ham.

Example usage:

# a sublattice mass switched on and off
drive = DrivenKSpace(ks, lambda k, t: ks.get_ham(k) + m * np.cos(w * t) * sz, 2 * np.pi / w)
get_evolution(k: ArrayLike, t: float | None = None) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

Get the evolution operator \(U(\mathbf{k}, t) = \mathcal{T}e^{-i\int_0^tH(\mathbf{k},t')dt'}\).

Parameters:

  • k – k point (see KSpace.get_ham).

  • t – Real number in \([0, T]\). Default value None (one period: the Floquet operator \(U(\mathbf{k}, T)\)).

Returns:

  • U – Complex ndarray, shape (norb, norb).

get_ham(k: ArrayLike) → NDArray[complex128][source]#

Get the Floquet Hamiltonian \(H_F(\mathbf{k})\), quasienergies in \([\epsilon_{cut} - \omega, \epsilon_{cut})\) (default \([-\omega/2, \omega/2)\)).

Parameters:

k – k point (see KSpace.get_ham).

Returns:

  • H_F – Complex ndarray, shape (norb, norb).

is_hermitian() → bool[source]#

The Floquet Hamiltonian of a Hermitian drive is Hermitian.

winding_number(epsilon: float, nk: int | tuple[int, int] = 48, n_t: int = 40) → float[source]#

Get the winding number of Rudner, Lindner, Berg and Levin (Phys. Rev. X 3, 031005 (2013)), the number of chiral edge states in the quasienergy gap at epsilon:

\[W[U_\epsilon] = \frac{1}{8\pi^2}\int_0^T dt\int_{BZ} dk_x dk_y\, \mathrm{Tr}\left(U_\epsilon^{-1}\partial_tU_\epsilon \left[U_\epsilon^{-1}\partial_{k_x}U_\epsilon, U_\epsilon^{-1}\partial_{k_y}U_\epsilon\right]\right),\]

of the loop \(U_\epsilon(\mathbf{k}, t) = U(\mathbf{k}, 2t)\) for \(t \le T/2\), then \(V_\epsilon(\mathbf{k}, 2T - 2t)\), with the return map \(V_\epsilon(\mathbf{k}, t) = e^{-iH_F^\epsilon(\mathbf{k})t}\) and \(H_F^\epsilon\) the Floquet Hamiltonian with its branch cut at epsilon (see effective_hamiltonian). As the integrand is a 3-form, this is the winding of \(U\) over \([0, T]\) minus that of \(V_\epsilon\) over \([0, T]\).

Signs. \(W\) counts the chiral edge states in the gap: \(W = n_{lower} = -n_{upper}\) of edge_state_count, so \(W > 0\) means states moving along \(+\mathbf{a}_1\) on the edge of a ribbon on the side of \(-\hat{z}\times\mathbf{a}_1\) (the bottom edge of a ribbon along x). Across a group of Floquet bands, \(W[U_{\epsilon'}] - W[U_\epsilon] = -\sum_n C_n\) for \(\epsilon < \epsilon'\), the sum over the bands between the two gaps, with the Chern numbers \(C_n\) of chern_number (the paper’s \(\mathcal{C}_n = -\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\nabla\times\mathcal{A}_n\) is minus ours, so there \(W' - W = +\sum\mathcal{C}\)). A static model (whose bands fit in the zone below the cut) has \(W = 0\) at the zone edge, and \(W = -\sum C\) of the bands below any other gap. The anomalous phases are those with \(W \ne 0\) in every gap while all the \(C_n = 0\).

Discretization: \(U(\mathbf{k}, t)\) on a uniform \(n_1\times n_2\) Brillouin-zone grid, differentiated spectrally in \(\mathbf{k}\) (exponentially accurate: both \(U\) and, while the gap at epsilon is open, \(V_\epsilon\) are analytic and periodic in \(\mathbf{k}\)), and \(\partial_tU = -iHU\) exactly, integrated by Gauss-Legendre quadrature on each time step (n_t nodes per period in total, at least 2 per step) and over \([0, T]\) for the return map. Step drives are exact; a continuous drive is replaced by its n_steps midpoint steps, whose loop has the same \(W\) as long as the gap stays open.

Tolerance. The result is returned raw. Its error falls off exponentially with nk, at a rate set by the k-width of the region where \(V_\epsilon\) varies fast, gap / band velocity near the smallest gap at epsilon (the Berry curvature is concentrated there). For the five-step model (\(\delta_{AB} = 0.5\pi/T\)) the error is below \(10^{-12}\) at perfect transfer; with a gap of \(0.067\omega\) it is \(2\times10^{-5}\) at the default nk = 48; with a gap of \(0.021\omega\) it is \(10^{-2}\) at nk = 48 and \(4\times10^{-4}\) at nk = 96. Circularly driven graphene (gap \(0.01\omega\) at K) needs nk = 96 for \(3\times10^{-3}\). Rounding to the nearest integer is trustworthy when \(|W - \mathrm{round}(W)| < 0.01\) and the value is unchanged within that tolerance when nk is doubled; a value far from an integer means the gap is too small for the grid (or closed).

Parameters:

  • epsilon – Real number. Quasienergy of the gap (branch cut).

  • nk – Positive integer (at least 4), or tuple of 2. Default value 48. k-points along each reciprocal vector.

  • n_t – Positive integer. Default value 40. Gauss-Legendre nodes per period (at least 2 per step; 2 n_t, and at least 24, for the return map).

Returns:

  • W – Real number, close to an integer.

edge_state_count(epsilon: float, nk: int = 200, window: float | None = None) → tuple[float, float][source]#

Count the chiral edge states of a driven ribbon (a 1D model, e.g. made by step_drive from kspace.ribbon models) crossing the quasienergy gap at epsilon, on each of its two edges.

Following the quasienergies \(\epsilon_n(k)\) over the Brillouin zone (\(k\) along \(\mathbf{a}_1\), nk points), a state crossing epsilon upwards (\(d\epsilon/dk > 0\)) counts +1, downwards -1, weighted by its probability on each half of the ribbon (the halves below and above its middle line, along \(\hat{z}\times\mathbf{a}_1\)). States are followed from one k to the next by their largest overlap. Only states within window of epsilon are followed; bulk states do not cross a gap, so only edge states contribute. The counts are integers, \(\pm1\) per chiral mode, up to the tail of the edge states on the other half (exponentially small in the width) and the two edges sum to zero. With the conventions of winding_number, n_upper = -n_lower = W (checked in the tests and examples).

Parameters:

  • epsilon – Real number. Quasienergy of the gap.

  • nk – Positive integer (at least 4). Default value 200. k-points, fine enough that a state moves by less than window between two.

  • window – Positive real. Default value None (\(\omega/8\)).

Returns:

  • n_lower – Real number. Signed count on the lower edge.

  • n_upper – Real number. Signed count on the upper edge.

class tbkit.floquet.FloquetKSpace(ks, vector_potential: Callable, period: float, n_steps: int = 100, epsilon: float | None = None)[source]#

Bases: DrivenKSpace

A periodic model driven by a uniform, time-periodic vector potential \(\mathbf{A}(t)\) (e.g. circularly polarized light, \(\mathbf{A}(t) = A_0(\cos\omega t, \sin\omega t)\)), coupled through the Peierls phases of its bonds (see KSpace.get_ham_peierls).

It is a copy of the KSpace model whose get_ham returns the Floquet Hamiltonian \(H_F(\mathbf{k})\) (see effective_hamiltonian), so get_bands, k_path, berry_curvature, chern_number, wannier_centers, … describe the driven system (quasienergies in the first Floquet zone: for Chern numbers, pick bands separated by gaps that do not wrap around the zone edge, or move the zone edge with epsilon). It is a DrivenKSpace, with \(H(\mathbf{k}, t)\) = ks.get_ham_peierls(k, vector_potential(t)), so winding_number applies. Real-space methods that need static hoppings (finite_ham, get_ham_beta, gbz) are not available.

Parameters:

  • ks – KSpace instance (the static model).

  • vector_potential – Callable. vector_potential(t) returns \(\mathbf{A}(t)\) (space_dim components).

  • period – Positive real. \(T\).

  • n_steps – Positive integer. Default value 100. Time steps per period.

  • epsilon – Real number. Default value None (quasienergies in \([-\omega/2, \omega/2)\), as before this option existed). Branch cut of get_ham, see effective_hamiltonian.

is_hermitian() → bool[source]#

The Floquet Hamiltonian of a Hermitian drive is Hermitian.

Check that bands are separated from the other bands by a line gap: with the bands ordered by keys (Re E or Im E, shape (nk, norb)) at every k-point, a band inside the group and its neighbour outside it never overlap over the whole mesh.

Raises:

ValueError – The bands have no line gap.

tbkit.error_handling.band_continuity(en, bands)[source]#

Check that a group of bands, labelled at every point of a periodic k mesh (en, complex, shape (n1, n2, norb)), is continuous: matching the eigenvalues of neighbouring points by distance maps the group onto itself. A line gap measured on the mesh alone can miss a narrow crossing between mesh points; this catches the jump of the labels.

Raises:

ValueError – The band labels jump between neighbouring k-points.
